knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer complexity when every additive error is uniformly absorbable into the residual decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\delta_k\le\theta c\|\widetilde G_k\|^2\) with a fixed \(\theta<1\), the inexact descent estimate has effective decrease constant \((1-\theta)c\). Consequently, \[\min_{0\le k<N}\|\widetilde G_k\|\le\sqrt{\frac{\varphi(x_0)-\varphi_{\inf}}{(1-\theta)cN}},\] and the outer bound remains \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative subproblem error uniformly smaller than the residual decrease preserves the order epsilon-to-the-minus-two outer bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Error Complexity Preservation

assumptions_latex: The available estimate is \(\varphi(x_k)-\varphi(x_{k+1})\ge c\|\widetilde G_k\|^2-\delta\) with fixed \(c>0\) and \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The estimate permits \(\|\widetilde G_k\|=\sqrt{\delta/c}\) for every \(k\), so it cannot certify tolerances below \(\sqrt{\delta/c}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical residual floor under a nonvanishing additive inexactness allowance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A constant additive allowance \(\delta>0\) is compatible with a constant objective sequence and \(\|\widetilde G_k\|=\sqrt{\delta/c}\) at every iteration. Thus the descent estimate alone permits a nonzero residual floor and gives no arbitrary-accuracy complexity guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed additive solve error permits a nonzero residual indefinitely, so arbitrary accuracy requires a vanishing, summable, or absorbable error budget.
knowledge_statements.title: Persistent-Error Residual Floor

assumptions_latex: Computed residuals satisfy \(\varphi(x_k)-\varphi(x_{k+1})\ge c\|\widetilde G_k\|^2-\delta_k\) with \(c>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer successful-iteration complexity under additive, summably controlled subproblem errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Summation of the inexact descent inequalities yields \[c\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\|\widetilde G_k\|^2\le\varphi(x_0)-\varphi(x_N)+D_N\le\varphi(x_0)-\varphi_{\inf}+D_N.\] Hence \[\min_{0\le k<N}\|\widetilde G_k\|\le\sqrt{\frac{\varphi(x_0)-\varphi_{\inf}+D_N}{cN}}.\] If \(\sup_N D_N<\infty\), the outer iteration bound remains \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) for finding \(\|\widetilde G_k\|\le\varepsilon\). This bound counts inexact subproblem calls, not their internal oracle complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summable additive subproblem errors preserve the order epsilon-to-the-minus-two outer complexity, with the constant enlarged by accumulated error.
knowledge_statements.title: Inexact-Subproblem Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-horizon inequality is mathematically consistent and the complexity-bound kind fits. The asymptotic order claim requires the separately stated uniform bound \(\sup_N D_N<\infty\), since finiteness of each finite partial sum alone is insufficient. No source supports the inexact prox-linear interpretation or error model.

children.title: Error-Bound Regimes
children.top_down_role: Residual-to-solution-set growth conditions relevant to prox-linear rates.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\|G_t(x)\|^\theta\) for all \(x\in U\); the case \(\theta=1\) is the linear error-bound regime.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hölder extension of the fixed-parameter prox-linear residual error-bound regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local Hölder prox-linear error bound of exponent \(\theta\in(0,1]\) holds on \(U\) when \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\|G_t(x)\|^\theta\qquad(x\in U).\] The case \(\theta=1\) is the local linear error bound. Requiring the inequality on the full domain gives the corresponding global regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hölder error bound controls distance by a positive power of the residual; exponent one recovers the linear regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Hölder Residual Error-Bound Regimes

assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=x^3/3\) and the nonsmooth term is zero.
The smooth-composite residual is \(G_t(x)=\nabla f(x)=x^2\), with zero set \(S=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth-composite obstruction showing that an isolated stationary point need not satisfy a linear residual error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the smooth composite \(f(x)=x^3/3\), the residual is \(G_t(x)=x^2\) and its zero set is \(S=\{0\}\). No finite \(\kappa\) satisfies \(|x|\le\kappa x^2\) throughout a neighborhood of zero, while the Hölder relation \(|x|=|G_t(x)|^{1/2}\) holds exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An isolated stationary point can have a quadratically vanishing residual, precluding a linear error bound while retaining a square-root Hölder bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratically Flat Residual Boundary

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a neighborhood of \(S\), and \(t>0\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local metric error bound expressed through the prox-linear residual.

source_refs.locator: 5.10 Residues and Error Bounds p. 475

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local prox-linear error-bound regime holds at the stationary set \(S\) when there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(S\) and a constant \(\kappa>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\|G_t(x)\|\qquad\text{for all }x\in U.\] A level-set version replaces \(U\) by \(U\cap\{x:\varphi(x)\le a\}\) for a specified level \(a\). The constants \(t\), \(\kappa\), and the neighborhood are part of the regime and must remain fixed when the condition is used for a local rate claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local error bound controls distance to the stationary set by a fixed multiple of the prox-linear residual throughout a specified neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 5.10 Residues and Error Bounds p. 475

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement is a coherent local residual error-bound condition and its content kind fits the leaf. The cited LCP chapter may support residual error bounds generally, but it does not establish that the prox-linear residual \(G_t\) and stationary set used here fall under that result. A prox-linear-specific source or an explicit specialization reference is required.

children.title: Quadratic-Growth Regimes
children.top_down_role: Objective-growth conditions relevant to local stability or convergence rates.

assumptions_latex: \(S=\mathop{\rm argmin}\varphi\) is nonempty, with minimum value \(\varphi_\star\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local quadratic growth relative to the complete minimizer set.

source_refs.locator: 4.4.2 Piecewise linear-quadratic functions p. 198

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The objective \(\varphi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) has local quadratic growth around its solution set \(S\) if there exist \(\mu>0\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(S\) such that \[\varphi(x)\ge\varphi_\star+\frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2\qquad\text{for every }x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}\varphi.\] A level-restricted regime requires the same inequality only for points additionally satisfying \(\varphi(x)\le a\), where \(a>\varphi_\star\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic growth means objective suboptimality locally dominates a positive constant times squared distance to the full solution set.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Growth Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 4.4.2 Piecewise linear-quadratic functions p. 198

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\{0\}\times\mathbb R\) and \(f(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2\), but \(f\) is not strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes solution-set quadratic growth from strong convexity and isolated minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2\), the minimizer set is \(S=\{0\}\times\mathbb R\) and \(f(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2\), so global quadratic growth holds with modulus \(\mu=2\). The function is constant along the \(x_2\)-direction and therefore is not strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic growth relative to the full minimizer set does not imply strong convexity or an isolated minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Growth Without Strong Convexity

children.title: Growth-to-Error-Bound Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Regularity settings linking quadratic growth with residual error bounds.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex, with \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\).
For a fixed \(t>0\), \(G_t=t^{-1}(I-\operatorname{prox}_{tf})\) satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\|G_t(x)\|\) throughout a neighborhood of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist a neighborhood \(V\) of \(S\) and \(\mu>0\) such that \(f(x)-\inf f\ge(\mu/2)\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2\) for every \(x\in V\cap\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential converse completing the local convex quadratic-growth/proximal-error-bound correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper closed convex function with nonempty minimizer set, a local error bound for the scaled proximal residual implies local quadratic growth. Specifically, if \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\|G_t(x)\|\) near \(S\), then, after possibly shrinking the neighborhood, there is \(\mu>0\) such that \[f(x)-\inf f\ge\frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex objective, a local proximal-residual error bound implies local quadratic objective growth, possibly on a smaller neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Error Bound Implies Quadratic Growth
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Error Bound Implies Quadratic Growth
Growth-to-Error-Bound Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex proximal-residual version of the local quadratic-growth correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, with nonempty minimizer set \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\). Suppose that \(f(x)-\inf f\geq \frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}^2(x,S)\) on a neighborhood \(U\) of \(S\), where \(\mu>0\). For \(t>0\), define \(P_t=\operatorname{prox}_{tf}\) and \(G_t=t^{-1}(I-P_t)\). If \(x,P_t(x)\in U\), then \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq(t+2/\mu)\lVert G_t(x)\rVert\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper closed convex objective with local quadratic growth, the scaled proximal residual locally bounds distance to the minimizer set with constant t plus 2 divided by mu.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex, with \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\).
For a neighborhood \(U\) of \(S\) and \(\mu>0\), \(f(x)-\inf f\geq\frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}^2(x,S)\) for every \(x\in U\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: convex quadratic growth and proximal optimality give the stated local residual error bound
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Sharpness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Local growth structures supporting enhanced prox-linear behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\) is an isolated unconstrained local minimizer of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No \(\alpha>0\) satisfies \(f(x)-f(\bar x)\ge\alpha\|x-\bar x\|\) throughout a neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order obstruction to positive linear sharpness at a differentiable unconstrained isolated minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A differentiable function cannot have a positive linear sharpness modulus at an isolated unconstrained local minimizer. Thus \(|x|\) is sharp at zero, whereas the differentiable quadratic \(x^2\) is not linearly sharp there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive linear sharpness at an isolated unconstrained minimum requires nonsmooth first-order growth; a differentiable minimum is too flat.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Isolated-Minimum Sharpness Boundary

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f^\star\ge(\alpha/r)\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2\) on the same tube, corresponding to quadratic-growth modulus \(2\alpha/r\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local hierarchy showing that linear sharpness dominates quadratic growth on a fixed bounded tube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f(x)-f^\star\ge\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\) whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le r\), then on the same tube \[f(x)-f^\star\ge\frac{\alpha}{r}\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2.\] Under the convention \((\mu/2)\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2\), the resulting quadratic-growth modulus is \(\mu=2\alpha/r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear sharpness is stronger than quadratic growth on every fixed tube around the solution set.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness Dominates Quadratic Growth Locally

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, and \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sharpness modulus on \(U\) is \(\operatorname{sha}_U(f)=\sup\{\mu\geq0:f(x)-f^\star\geq\mu\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\ \forall x\in U\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weak sharp minima are defined by linear objective growth away from the solution set
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local weak-sharp-minimum regime, including its quantitative modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The objective \(f\) is sharp on \(U\) with modulus \(\mu\) when \(f(x)-f^\star\geq\mu\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\) for every \(x\in U\). The regime is global when \(U=\mathbb{R}^n\), local when \(U\) is only a neighborhood of \(S\), and uniform along a subset \(S_0\subset S\) when one neighborhood and one positive modulus work for every point of \(S_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sharpness means that objective excess grows at least linearly with distance from the solution set, locally or globally.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness Regimes

children.title: Active-Manifold Identification
children.top_down_role: Finite or asymptotic recognition of locally active smooth structure.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.

\(f\) is partly smooth at \(\bar x\) relative to a \(C^2\) manifold \(\mathcal M\), with \(f|_{\mathcal M}\) smooth, \(\partial f\) continuous relative to \(\mathcal M\), and \(\operatorname{par}\partial f(\bar x)=N_{\mathcal M}(\bar x)\).
\(x_k\to\bar x\), \(v_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), \(v_k\to\bar v\), and \(\bar v\in\operatorname{ri}\partial f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(K\) such that \(x_k\in\mathcal M\) for every \(k\ge K\).

notation.meaning: Active smooth manifold at the limiting point
Parallel subspace of a convex set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite identification for the convex-subdifferential formulation of partial smoothness and strict complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be proper, closed, convex, and partly smooth at \(\bar x\) relative to \(\mathcal M\) in the stated sense. If \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(v_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), \(v_k\to\bar v\), and \(\bar v\in\operatorname{ri}\partial f(\bar x)\), then the sequence identifies the active manifold: \(x_k\in\mathcal M\) for all sufficiently large \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex partly smooth function, subgradient graph convergence to a relative-interior certificate forces finite identification of the active manifold.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Partial-Smoothness Identification

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is partly smooth at \(\bar x\) relative to a \(C^2\) manifold \(\mathcal M\).
The nondegeneracy condition \(\bar v\in\operatorname{ri}\partial f(\bar x)\) holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(K\) such that \(x_k\in\mathcal M\) for every \(k\geq K\).

notation.meaning: Active smooth manifold at the limiting point.
Relative interior of a convex set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite identification under partial smoothness and strict complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that partial smoothness includes smoothness of \(f|_{\mathcal M}\), sharpness of the normal geometry, and continuity of \(\partial f\) relative to \(\mathcal M\) near \(\bar x\). If \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(v_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), \(v_k\to\bar v\), and \(\bar v\in\operatorname{ri}\partial f(\bar x)\), then the sequence identifies the active manifold: there is an index \(K<\infty\) such that \(x_k\in\mathcal M\) for all \(k\geq K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subgradient convergence to a nondegenerate limiting subgradient forces all sufficiently late iterates onto the partly smooth active manifold.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Manifold Identification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A source is required to determine the precise subdifferential, partial-smoothness definition, function-value or graph-convergence assumptions, and nondegeneracy condition needed for this identification theorem. The stated hypotheses may be insufficient under some standard variants.

children.title: Sharpness-Driven Identification
children.top_down_role: Geometric conditions connecting sharp growth to reliable manifold identification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharpness Separates Nonsolution Subgradients from Zero
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative convex subgradient separation underlying finite solution-set identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\), and suppose \(f(x)-f^\star\geq\mu\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\) for every \(x\in U\). If \(x\in U\setminus S\), \(p\in P_S(x)\), and \(v\in\partial f(x)\), then \(\langle v,x-p\rangle\geq f(x)-f^\star\geq\mu\|x-p\|\). Consequently, \(\|v\|\geq\mu\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\geq\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every subgradient at a nonsolution point in a convex sharpness neighborhood has norm at least the sharpness modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex with nonempty minimizer set \(S\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean projections of x onto the minimizer set.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness Separates Nonsolution Subgradients from Zero
Sharpness-Driven Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite solution-set identification from convex sharpness and vanishing subgradient residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, with \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\) and \(f^\star=\inf f\). Suppose that \(f(x)-f^\star\geq\mu\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\) on a neighborhood \(U\) of \(S\), where \(\mu>0\). If \(x_k\in U\), \(v_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), and \(\lVert v_k\rVert\to0\), then there exists \(K\) such that \(x_k\in S\) for every \(k\geq K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex sharp objective, any sequence in the sharpness neighborhood with vanishing selected subgradients enters the solution set after finitely many terms.
assumptions_latex: For a neighborhood \(U\) of \(S\), \(f(x)-f^\star\geq\mu\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\) holds for every \(x\in U\), where \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(K\) such that \(x_k\in S\) for every \(k\geq K\).

notation.meaning: Selected convex subgradient at the kth iterate.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: convex sharpness separates nonsolution subgradient norms from zero

children.title: Identification Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Degeneracy, inexactness, or instability regimes preventing persistent active-structure recognition.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_k,v_k)\to(0,1)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\), but \(1\notin\operatorname{ri}\partial f(0)\) and \(x_k\notin\mathcal M\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-complementarity boundary: subgradient graph convergence does not identify the manifold when the limiting certificate lies on the relative boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=|x|\), take \(x_k=1/k\) and \(v_k=1\in\partial f(x_k)\). Then \((x_k,v_k)\to(0,1)\), but \(1\) lies on the relative boundary of \(\partial f(0)=[-1,1]\). The points never enter \(\mathcal M=\{0\}\), so subgradient graph convergence without the relative-interior condition does not force identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergent subgradient certificates need not identify the active manifold when their limit lies on the boundary of the limiting subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Certificate Identification Failure
Identification Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by absent subgradient convergence to a nondegenerate limiting certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=|x|\), the function is partly smooth at \(0\) relative to \(\mathcal M=\{0\}\), and \(0\in\operatorname{ri}\partial f(0)\). Nevertheless, \(x_k=1/k\) satisfies \(x_k\to0\) and \(f(x_k)\to f(0)\) while \(x_k\notin\mathcal M\) for every \(k\). The selections \(v_k=1\in\partial f(x_k)\) do not converge to \(0\), showing that iterate and value convergence alone do not ensure active-manifold identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the absolute-value function, convergence of points and values to zero does not identify the singleton active manifold when the required subgradients fail to converge to the limiting certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=|x|\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), with minimizer \(0\) and active manifold \(\mathcal M=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(x_k\to0\) and \(f(x_k)\to f(0)\), one has \(x_k\notin\mathcal M\) for every \(k\), and \(v_k\not\to0\).

notation.meaning: Singleton active manifold at the minimizer.
Sequence approaching zero from the positive side.

children.title: Loss of Model Convexity or Prox-Regularity

knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Model Convexity or Prox-Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonunique proximal step produced by loss of model convexity and prox-regular behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t>0\), let \(m(y)=-|y|+|y|^2/(2t)\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). Then \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{R}}m(y)=\{-t,t\}\). Thus quadratic regularization does not make this nonconvex model uniquely solvable, and it does not induce a canonical single-valued model residual or envelope gradient at the base point without a selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex model can retain two proximal minimizers after quadratic regularization, preventing a canonical single-valued residual or envelope gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{R}}m(y)=\{-t,t\}\), so the model step is not single-valued.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct minimization of the displayed one-dimensional model establishes nonuniqueness
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Uncontrolled Linearization Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of quadratic model accuracy when the derivative is not locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c(x)=|x|^{3/2}\). Then \(c\) is continuously differentiable and \(c(0)=c'(0)=0\), but for every finite \(L\) and every neighborhood \(U\) of \(0\), there exists \(y\in U\) such that \(|c(y)-c(0)-c'(0)y|>\frac{L}{2}|y|^2\). Hence no uniform local quadratic linearization-error bound holds at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The continuously differentiable map absolute x to the three-halves power has no uniform quadratic linearization-error bound at zero.
assumptions_latex: \(c(x)=|x|^{3/2}\), and the linearization is taken at \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(L<\infty\), the estimate \(|c(y)-c(0)-c'(0)y|\leq\frac{L}{2}|y|^2\) fails arbitrarily near \(0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the explicit error ratio diverges near zero
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Residual Jacobians
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of a linear error bound at a singular residual Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=x^2\), \(S=F^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\), and \(r(x)=|F(x)|\). Since \(F'(0)=0\), no finite \(\kappa\) and neighborhood \(U\) of \(0\) satisfy \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\) for every \(x\in U\). Thus this degenerate residual Jacobian destroys a local linear residual error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the equation x squared equals zero, the singular residual Jacobian is accompanied by failure of every local linear error bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No \(\kappa<\infty\) and neighborhood \(U\) of \(0\) satisfy \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa r(x)\) for every \(x\in U\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the explicit scalar example directly disproves a local linear residual error bound
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Model Decrease without Objective Progress
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit mismatch between proximal-model decrease and true composite-objective progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(z)=z\), \(c(y)=y^2+1\), \(f=h\circ c\), and take the base point \(x=1\) with proximal parameter \(t=3/2\). The regularized linearized model is \(m_x(y)=2y+(y-1)^2/3\), whose unique minimizer is \(y=-2\). At this point, \(m_x(-2)=-1<m_x(1)=2\), whereas \(f(-2)=5>f(1)=2\). Thus exact model decrease need not imply objective decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact minimizer of a regularized linearized model can lower that model while increasing the true composite objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique model minimizer is \(y=-2\), with \(m_x(-2)<m_x(1)\) but \(f(-2)>f(1)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct evaluation verifies strict model decrease and strict objective increase
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact-Subproblem Error Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute subproblem errors can dominate the available model improvement near a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=|x|\), \(t>0\), and \(0<x<t\). For the proximal subproblem \(q_x(y)=|y|+(y-x)^2/(2t)\), the exact minimizer is \(y^\star=0\). Under an absolute objective-gap tolerance \(\varepsilon\), the zero step \(y=x\) is admissible whenever \(\varepsilon\geq x-x^2/(2t)\). Hence an error tolerance comparable to the available model decrease can admit no progress at a nonstationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An absolute proximal-subproblem tolerance can admit a zero step at a nonstationary point when the tolerance dominates the available model decrease.
assumptions_latex: An inexact solver accepts \(y\) whenever its proximal-objective gap is at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\varepsilon\geq x-x^2/(2t)\), then \(y=x\) is admissible although the exact proximal point is \(0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the proximal objective gap is explicit and directly verifies admissibility of the zero step
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Firmly Nonexpansive Residuals
children.top_down_role: Residual structure induced by firmly nonexpansive fixed-point maps.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse residual inheritance completing complement symmetry of firm nonexpansiveness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(T:H\to H\), and set \(R=I-T\). If \(R\) is firmly nonexpansive, then \(T=I-R\) is firmly nonexpansive. Therefore \(T\) is firmly nonexpansive if and only if its residual \(I-T\) is firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Firm nonexpansiveness is preserved in both directions by taking the complementary residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T=I-R\) is firmly nonexpansive; hence \(T\) is firmly nonexpansive if and only if \(I-T\) is firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.title: Converse Firmness of the Complement
Firmly Nonexpansive Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual inheritance of firmness for Hilbert-space fixed-point mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(T:H\to H\) be firmly nonexpansive. Then the residual \(R=I-T\) is firmly nonexpansive: for all \(x,y\in H\), \(\lVert Rx-Ry\rVert^2\leq\langle Rx-Ry,x-y\rangle\). Consequently, \(R\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz, and \(R(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The residual of a firmly nonexpansive fixed-point map is firmly nonexpansive, one-Lipschitz, and vanishes exactly at fixed points.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(T:H\to H\) is firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is firmly nonexpansive and therefore \(1\)-Lipschitz, with \(R^{-1}(0)=\operatorname{Fix}T\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the complement of a firmly nonexpansive operator is firmly nonexpansive
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Averaged Residuals
children.top_down_role: Residual structure across averaged fixed-point maps.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness of the universal cocoercivity and Lipschitz constants for alpha-averaged mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(0<\alpha<1\) on a nonzero real Hilbert space and take \(N=-I\). Then \(T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha N=(1-2\alpha)I\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged and \(R=I-T=2\alpha I\). The largest \(\beta\) for which \(R\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive is \(\beta=(2\alpha)^{-1}\), and the exact Lipschitz modulus of \(R\) is \(2\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxed reflection attains both universal averaged-residual constants, so neither can be improved.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a nonzero real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimal cocoercivity constant of \(R\) is \((2\alpha)^{-1}\), and \(\operatorname{Lip}(R)=2\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Exact global Lipschitz modulus of R.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of Averaged-Residual Constants
Averaged Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cocoercivity and Lipschitz control of residuals of averaged operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha N\), where \(0<\alpha<1\) and \(N:H\to H\) is nonexpansive. For \(R=I-T\) and all \(x,y\in H\), \(\langle Rx-Ry,x-y\rangle\geq(2\alpha)^{-1}\lVert Rx-Ry\rVert^2\). Consequently, \(R\) is \((2\alpha)^{-1}\)-cocoercive and \(2\alpha\)-Lipschitz, and \(R(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The residual of an alpha-averaged mapping is one-over-two-alpha cocoercive, two-alpha Lipschitz, and vanishes exactly at fixed points.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha N\), where \(0<\alpha<1\) and \(N:H\to H\) is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For all \(x,y\in H\), \(\langle Rx-Ry,x-y\rangle\geq\frac{1}{2\alpha}\lVert Rx-Ry\rVert^2\) and \(\lVert Rx-Ry\rVert\leq2\alpha\lVert x-y\rVert\), with \(R^{-1}(0)=\operatorname{Fix}T\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the standard characterization of averaged operators gives cocoercivity of their residuals

children.title: Firmness-to-Averagedness Residual Transfer
children.top_down_role: Transfer boundaries between the two residual classes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General Averaged Maps Lack the Strong Firmness-Transfer Constant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary between arbitrary averaged maps and relaxations of firmly nonexpansive maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0<\alpha<1\) on a nonzero real Hilbert space, set \(N=-I\), and define \(T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha N\). Then \(T\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged and \(R_T=2\alpha I\), whose largest cocoercivity constant is \((2\alpha)^{-1}\). Thus an arbitrary \(\alpha\)-averaged map need not have a \(1/\alpha\)-cocoercive residual; the stronger constant requires the representation \(T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha F\) with \(F\) firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The stronger residual constant transferred from a firm base map fails for general averaged maps.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a nonzero real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_T\) is not \(1/\alpha\)-cocoercive; its optimal cocoercivity constant is \(1/(2\alpha)\).

notation.meaning: Firmly nonexpansive base map in the stronger transfer regime.

knowledge_statements.title: General Averaged Maps Lack the Strong Firmness-Transfer Constant
Firmness-to-Averagedness Residual Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual scaling for a relaxation of a firmly nonexpansive Hilbert-space operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:H\to H\) be firmly nonexpansive, let \(0<\alpha<1\), and define \(T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha F\). Then \(T\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged and its residual satisfies \(R_T=I-T=\alpha(I-F)\). Because \(I-F\) is firmly nonexpansive, \(\alpha^{-1}R_T\) is firmly nonexpansive and, for all \(x,y\in H\), \[\langle R_Tx-R_Ty,x-y\rangle\geq \alpha^{-1}\|R_Tx-R_Ty\|^2.\] Thus firmness transfers to \(1/\alpha\)-cocoercivity of the averaged-operator residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing a firmly nonexpansive map scales its firmly nonexpansive residual by α, making the relaxed residual 1/α-cocoercive.

notation.meaning: identity operator on the Hilbert space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual identity and cocoercivity constant are mathematically consistent and the property kind fits the leaf, but no inspectable authoritative source is cited.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic Regularity Does Not Imply Convergence or Solvability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary of orbitwise asymptotic regularity without boundedness or a fixed-point hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=[0,\infty)\) with its usual metric, define \(T:X\to X\) by \(T(x)=x+(1+x)^{-1}\), and set \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k\). Every orbit satisfies \(x_{k+1}-x_k=(1+x_k)^{-1}\to0\), but \(x_k\to+\infty\) and \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successive differences can vanish even while the orbit diverges and the mapping has no fixed point.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Regularity Does Not Imply Convergence or Solvability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Averaged Picard Orbits Are Asymptotically Regular
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative asymptotic regularity of Picard iteration for an averaged map having a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(T:H\to H\) be \(\alpha\)-averaged with \(0<\alpha<1\), assume \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\), and set \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k\). For every \(z\in\operatorname{Fix}T\), \[\|x_{k+1}-z\|^2\leq\|x_k-z\|^2-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|^2.\] Consequently, \[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|^2\leq\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\|x_0-z\|^2,\qquad \|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\to0,\] and \[\min_{0\leq j\leq k}\|(I-T)x_j\|\leq\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{(1-\alpha)(k+1)}}\,\|x_0-z\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Picard iteration of an averaged map with a fixed point has square-summable displacements and a best-iterate residual bound of order one over the square root of the iteration count.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_k\|(I-T)x_k\|^2<\infty\), hence \(\|(I-T)x_k\|\to0\), with the displayed \(O(k^{-1/2})\) best-iterate bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Averaged Picard Orbits Are Asymptotically Regular
Asymptotic Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbitwise asymptotic regularity for a fixed-point iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\) and generate an orbit by \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k\). The orbit is asymptotically regular when \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|=0.\] Equivalently, with the residual \(R_T=I-T\), asymptotic regularity means \(\|R_Tx_k\|\to0\). The operator \(T\) is asymptotically regular at \(x_0\) if its orbit from \(x_0\) has this property, and asymptotically regular if this holds for every \(x_0\in H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-point orbit is asymptotically regular when successive iterates, equivalently their fixed-point residuals, converge to zero.

notation.meaning: orbit generated by repeated application of \(T\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The orbitwise and operator-level definitions are precise and mutually consistent, but the record supplies no source with a specific locator.

children.title: Fixed-Point Solution Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificates expressed at splitting fixed points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Posteriori Distance Certificate for Contractions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-to-solution distance conversion when the fixed-point map is contractive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Banach space and let \(T:H\to H\) be a contraction with modulus \(0\le q<1\). Let \(x^*\) be its unique fixed point. Then every \(z\in H\) satisfies \[\|z-x^*\|\leq\frac{\|z-Tz\|}{1-q}.\] Consequently, \(\|R_Tz\|\leq\varepsilon\) certifies \(\|z-x^*\|\leq\varepsilon/(1-q)\). The factor \((1-q)^{-1}\) is sharp, as shown by \(T(x)=qx\) on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a contraction, the computable fixed-point residual gives a sharp a posteriori bound on distance to the unique fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \(x^*\) is the unique fixed point of T.
knowledge_statements.title: A Posteriori Distance Certificate for Contractions
Fixed-Point Solution Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and approximate certificates based on a computable fixed-point residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a normed space, let \(T:H\to H\), and define \(R_T=I-T\). For \(z\in H\), the equality \(R_Tz=0\) is an exact fixed-point certificate, since it is equivalent to \(z\in\operatorname{Fix}T\). For \(\varepsilon\geq0\), the inequality \(\|R_Tz\|\leq\varepsilon\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-fixed-point certificate. If \(X\) is a set, \(S\subseteq X\), and a recovery map \(P:H\to X\) satisfies \(P(\operatorname{Fix}T)\subseteq S\), then \(R_Tz=0\) also certifies \(Pz\in S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero fixed-point residual exactly certifies a fixed point, while a residual bounded by epsilon certifies an approximate fixed point. Under a stated recovery correspondence, an exact fixed point also certifies membership of the recovered point in the target solution set.
assumptions_latex: For the recovery claim, \(X\) is a set, \(S\subseteq X\), and \(P:H\to X\) satisfies \(P(\operatorname{Fix}T)\subseteq S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_Tz=0\iff z\in\operatorname{Fix}T\); under the recovery correspondence, \(R_Tz=0\Rightarrow Pz\in S\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-point encoding of a monotone inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines fixed-point encoding and records the failure of naive forward–forward and backward–backward compositions to encode zeros of an operator sum in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the monotone inclusion \(0\in(\mathbb A+\mathbb B)x\), a fixed-point encoding is a related operator \(T\) equipped with a correspondence between \(\operatorname{zer}(\mathbb A+\mathbb B)\) and \(\operatorname{Fix}T\) that permits recovery of an inclusion solution from a corresponding fixed point. When the displayed forward map is defined and \(\alpha\neq0\), \(\mathbb I-\alpha(\mathbb A+\mathbb B)\) is the ordinary forward-step map, rather than a distinct forward–forward splitting. In general, neither \((\mathbb I-\alpha\mathbb A)(\mathbb I-\beta\mathbb B)\) nor \(\mathbb J_{\alpha\mathbb A}\mathbb J_{\alpha\mathbb B}\) is a valid fixed-point encoding of \(0\in(\mathbb A+\mathbb B)x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-point encoding relates solutions of a monotone inclusion to fixed points of another operator so that a solution can be recovered. A forward step applied to the summed operator is simply the forward-step method. In general, composing separate forward steps or composing the two resolvents does not encode the zeros of the operator sum.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb A\) and \(\mathbb B\) define the inclusion \(0\in(\mathbb A+\mathbb B)x\).
The displayed forward maps and resolvents are well-defined; for \(\mathbb I-\alpha(\mathbb A+\mathbb B)\), \(\alpha\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The separate compositions \((\mathbb I-\alpha\mathbb A)(\mathbb I-\beta\mathbb B)\) and \(\mathbb J_{\alpha\mathbb A}\mathbb J_{\alpha\mathbb B}\) do not, in general, provide the fixed-point–solution correspondence required to recover an element of \(\operatorname{zer}(\mathbb A+\mathbb B)\).

children.title: Inclusion-Solution Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificates expressed at solutions of the underlying inclusion.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normwise inclusion certificate obtained by minimizing over graph witnesses at a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\), define \[\delta_{A+B}(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,Ax+Bx)=\inf\{\|a+b\|:a\in Ax,\ b\in Bx\},\] with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Then \(0\in Ax+Bx\) implies \(\delta_{A+B}(x)=0\). Conversely, if \(Ax+Bx\) is closed, \(\delta_{A+B}(x)=0\) implies \(0\in Ax+Bx\); without closedness it implies only \(0\in\overline{Ax+Bx}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smallest additive graph-witness residual is exact when the pointwise sum is closed; otherwise zero distance certifies only closure membership.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in Ax+Bx\Rightarrow\delta_{A+B}(x)=0\), and closedness of \(Ax+Bx\) gives the converse.

notation.meaning: distance from zero to the pointwise sum \(Ax+Bx\)

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Additive Inclusion Defect

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Infimal Defect Without an Inclusion Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness failure for an infimal additive-residual certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\mathbb R\), \(Ax=(0,1)\), and \(Bx=\{0\}\) for every \(x\). Then \(Ax+Bx=(0,1)\), so \(\delta_{A+B}(x)=0\), while \(0\notin Ax+Bx\). Hence \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed operator value may approach zero without containing it, so zero infimal defect need not certify a solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero Infimal Defect Without an Inclusion Solution
Inclusion-Solution Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-witness certificate for a two-operator inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a normed space and let \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\). A triple \((x,a,b)\in H^3\) is an exact certificate for \(0\in Ax+Bx\) when \(a\in Ax\), \(b\in Bx\), and \(a+b=0\). Moreover, \[x\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{there exist }a\in Ax\text{ and }b\in Bx\text{ such that }a+b=0.\] For \(\varepsilon\geq0\), witnesses satisfying \(a\in Ax\), \(b\in Bx\), and \(\|a+b\|\leq\varepsilon\) form an additive-residual certificate; without additional regularity assumptions, this does not assert a distance bound to the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solution of the sum inclusion is equivalent to the existence of opposing graph elements from the two operators. Witnesses whose sum has norm at most epsilon provide only an additive-residual certificate unless further regularity is assumed.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct unpacking of a sum inclusion

children.title: Fixed-Point-to-Inclusion Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Mappings, recoverability, and correspondence boundaries between solution representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point inclusion correspondence without assuming a single-valued resolvent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\), \(B:H\to H\), and \(\gamma>0\). With the possibly set-valued resolvent \(J_{\gamma A}=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}\), define \(T_\gamma x=J_{\gamma A}(x-\gamma Bx)\). Then \[x\in T_\gamma x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-\gamma Bx\in x+\gamma Ax\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0\in Ax+Bx.\] Thus \(\{x:x\in T_\gamma x\}=\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\). Single-valuedness is needed only to replace membership by the equation \(x=T_\gamma x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fixed-point–inclusion correspondence remains valid for a set-valued resolvent when fixed points are expressed by membership; single-valuedness is required only for an ordinary fixed-point equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Valued Resolvent Correspondence
Fixed-Point-to-Inclusion Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-backward fixed-point representation of a two-operator inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\), let \(B:H\to H\), and choose \(\gamma>0\) such that the resolvent \(J_{\gamma A}=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}\) is single-valued on the required domain. Define \(T_\gamma=J_{\gamma A}(I-\gamma B)\). Then \[x=T_\gamma x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-\gamma Bx\in x+\gamma Ax\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0\in Ax+Bx.\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{Fix}T_\gamma=\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fixed points of the forward-backward map are exactly the zeros of the underlying sum inclusion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The resolvent equivalence is mathematically consistent, and representation is the appropriate kind for this correspondence leaf, but no inspectable source is provided.

children.title: Metric Residuals
children.top_down_role: Residual measurements induced by non-Euclidean metrics.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semimetric Residual Can Miss a Nonzero Displacement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure when the metric operator is positive semidefinite but not positive definite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\mathbb R^2\), \(M=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\), and \(T(x_1,x_2)=(x_1,x_2+1)\). Then \(R_Tx=(0,-1)\neq0\) and \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\varnothing\), but \(\|R_Tx\|_M=0\) for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semidefinite metric can erase a nonzero displacement lying in its kernel.
knowledge_statements.title: Semimetric Residual Can Miss a Nonzero Displacement
Metric Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point residual magnitude in a strongly positive operator-induced metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(M:H\to H\) be bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive. The \(M\)-inner product and norm are \(\langle x,y\rangle_M=\langle Mx,y\rangle\) and \(\|x\|_M=\sqrt{\langle Mx,x\rangle}\). For \(T:H\to H\), its metric residual at \(x\) is \(R_Tx=x-Tx\), measured by \(\|R_Tx\|_M\). This residual vanishes exactly when \(x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metric residual is the fixed-point displacement measured in the norm induced by a strongly positive metric operator.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The induced metric and residual definition are internally consistent and correctly scoped to a strongly positive Hilbert-space metric, but no authoritative source with a locator is cited.

children.title: Preconditioned Residuals
children.top_down_role: Residual representations arising from operator preconditioning.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singular Scaling Produces a False Zero Residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of fixed-point detection when the scaling operator is singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\) and \(T(x_1,x_2)=(x_1,x_2+1)\) on \(\mathbb R^2\). Then \(P(x-Tx)=0\) for every \(x\), although \(x\neq Tx\) for every \(x\). Thus injectivity of the scaling operator is necessary for \(P(I-T)x=0\Rightarrow x=Tx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular scaling can erase part of a nonzero displacement and create false zero residuals.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular Scaling Produces a False Zero Residual

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graph Representation of the Preconditioned Residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph witness generated by a preconditioned forward-backward evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B:H\to H\), \(y=T_Px=J_{P^{-1}A}(x-P^{-1}Bx)\), and \(r_P(x)=P(x-y)\). Then \[r_P(x)-Bx\in Ay,\qquad r_P(x)\in Ay+Bx.\] At \(r_P(x)=0\), invertibility of \(P\) gives \(y=x\), hence \(-Bx\in Ax\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A preconditioned forward-backward residual combines an A-graph element at the resolvent point with B evaluated at the base point.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Representation of the Preconditioned Residual
Preconditioned Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Natural residual for a preconditioned forward-backward inclusion map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\), \(B:H\to H\), and let \(P:H\to H\) be bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive. Suppose \(J_{P^{-1}A}=(I+P^{-1}A)^{-1}\) is single-valued where evaluated. Define \(T_P=J_{P^{-1}A}(I-P^{-1}B)\) and the preconditioned residual \[r_P(x)=P(x-T_Px).\] Then \(r_P(x)=0\) if and only if \(x=T_Px\), equivalently \(0\in Ax+Bx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The preconditioned residual rescales the forward-backward displacement by the preconditioner and vanishes exactly at inclusion solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive.
\(J_{P^{-1}A}\) is single-valued on the required domain.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-set equivalence is algebraically consistent, but calling P(I-T_P) the preconditioned residual is convention-dependent and requires an inspectable source.

children.title: Metric-to-Preconditioner Calibration
children.top_down_role: Comparability and scaling boundaries across metric and preconditioned representations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Uniform Calibration Under Degenerating Spectra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of iteration-independent tolerance conversion without uniform spectral bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_n=\operatorname{diag}(1,n^{-1})\) and \(d_n=(0,1)\). Then \(\|d_n\|=1\), while \(\|d_n\|_{P_n}=n^{-1/2}\) and \(\|P_nd_n\|=n^{-1}\). Thus metric and scaled residuals can vanish while Euclidean displacement remains fixed when the lower spectral bound degenerates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a uniform positive lower spectral bound, small metric or scaled residuals do not uniformly imply small Euclidean displacement.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Uniform Calibration Under Degenerating Spectra

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complete Euclidean Calibration of Primal and Scaled Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided Euclidean comparisons induced by uniform spectral bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(mI\preccurlyeq P\preccurlyeq MI\), \(d_P=x-T_Px\), and \(r_P=Pd_P\), then \[m\|d_P\|\leq\|r_P\|\leq M\|d_P\|,\qquad \frac1{\sqrt M}\|r_P\|\leq\|r_P\|_{P^{-1}}\leq\frac1{\sqrt m}\|r_P\|.\] Together with \(\|d_P\|_P=\|r_P\|_{P^{-1}}\), these inequalities convert tolerances among primal Euclidean, primal metric, scaled Euclidean, and dual-metric residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform spectral bounds provide all two-sided tolerance conversions among displacement and scaled-residual normalizations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed two-sided norm comparisons hold uniformly.
knowledge_statements.title: Complete Euclidean Calibration of Primal and Scaled Residuals
Metric-to-Preconditioner Calibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal-dual metric calibration and Euclidean spectral bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P:H\to H\) be bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive, let \(T_P:H\to H\), and set \(d_P(x)=x-T_Px\) and \(r_P(x)=Pd_P(x)\). Then the primal metric displacement and dual metric residual agree exactly: \[\|d_P(x)\|_P=\|r_P(x)\|_{P^{-1}}.\] If additionally \(mI\preccurlyeq P\preccurlyeq MI\) for \(0<m\leq M<\infty\), then \[\sqrt m\,\|d_P(x)\|\leq\|d_P(x)\|_P\leq\sqrt M\,\|d_P(x)\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preconditioner scaling converts primal metric displacement exactly into a dual-metric residual, with Euclidean comparisons determined by spectral bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive.
\(mI\preccurlyeq P\preccurlyeq MI\) for the Euclidean bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x-T_Px\|_P=\|r_P(x)\|_{P^{-1}}\), with the stated spectral norm bounds.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The primal-dual norm identity and spectral comparisons are correct under the stated positivity and order bounds, and property fits the calibration leaf, but no source is cited.

notation.meaning: explicit inclusion residual at the trial point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of the forward-backward displacement into a stationarity certificate at the resolvent point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(y=J_{\gamma A}(x-\gamma Bx)\), the vector \(v=G_\gamma(x)+By-Bx\) belongs to \(Ay+By\). If \(B\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then \(\|v\|\le(1+\gamma L)\|G_\gamma(x)\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forward-backward residual produces an explicit inclusion residual at the trial point, controlled by the computed mapping norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Trial-Point Inclusion Certificate

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\gamma\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged with \(\alpha=2\beta/(4\beta-\gamma)\), and its fixed-point iteration converges weakly to a zero of \(A+B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard convergence regime for monotone forward-backward splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For maximally monotone \(A\), \(\beta\)-cocoercive \(B\), and \(0<\gamma<2\beta\), \(T_\gamma=J_{\gamma A}(I-\gamma B)\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged with \(\alpha=2\beta/(4\beta-\gamma)<1\). If a zero exists, \(x_{k+1}=T_\gamma x_k\) converges weakly to a zero of \(A+B\), and \(\sum_k\|x_k-T_\gamma x_k\|^2<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under cocoercivity and the standard stepsize bound, forward-backward splitting is averaged, weakly convergent, and has finite residual energy.
knowledge_statements.title: Forward-Backward Averagedness and Convergence
Forward-Backward Residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaled natural residual for a forward-backward splitting map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\), \(B:H\to H\), and \(\gamma>0\), with \(J_{\gamma A}\) single-valued where evaluated. The forward-backward operator and its scaled residual are \[T_\gamma=J_{\gamma A}(I-\gamma B),\qquad G_\gamma=\gamma^{-1}(I-T_\gamma).\] Hence \(G_\gamma(x)=\gamma^{-1}[x-J_{\gamma A}(x-\gamma Bx)]\), and \(G_\gamma(x)=0\) if and only if \(0\in Ax+Bx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The forward-backward residual is the step displacement divided by the stepsize and vanishes exactly at solutions of the sum inclusion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scaled forward-backward residual and its zero-set characterization are consistent, but the scaling convention and correspondence lack an authoritative cited source.

children.title: Douglas–Rachford Residuals
children.top_down_role: Residual certificates associated with Douglas–Rachford fixed-point maps.

assumptions_latex: \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) are maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Averaged-operator geometry of the Douglas-Rachford residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Douglas-Rachford map \(T_{\mathrm{DR}}=\tfrac12(I+R_BR_A)\) is firmly nonexpansive. For every \(z\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\), \(\|T_{\mathrm{DR}}x-z\|^2+\|D_{\mathrm{DR}}x\|^2\le\|x-z\|^2\). Consequently, the stationary iteration has summable squared residuals whenever a fixed point exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Douglas-Rachford map is firmly nonexpansive, giving Fejer decrease and finite residual energy.
knowledge_statements.title: Firm Nonexpansiveness and Residual Energy

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_{\gamma A}(\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}})=\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\), with fixed points reconstructed from compatible graph decompositions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shadow correspondence for the reflected-resolvent order fixed by the seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\) and \(p=J_{\gamma A}x\), then \((x-p)/\gamma\in Ap\), \((p-x)/\gamma\in Bp\), and \(0\in Ap+Bp\). Conversely, if \(a\in Ap\) and \(-a\in Bp\), then \(x=p+\gamma a\) is a Douglas-Rachford fixed point with shadow \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Douglas-Rachford fixed points encode solutions through their resolvent shadows, and compatible graph decompositions reconstruct fixed points.
knowledge_statements.title: Douglas-Rachford Shadow-Solution Correspondence
Douglas–Rachford Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Douglas–Rachford displacement for two maximal monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone, let \(\gamma>0\), and define \(J_A=J_{\gamma A}\), \(J_B=J_{\gamma B}\), \(R_A=2J_A-I\), and \(R_B=2J_B-I\). The Douglas–Rachford operator and residual are \[T_{\mathrm{DR}}=\tfrac12(I+R_BR_A),\qquad D_{\mathrm{DR}}=I-T_{\mathrm{DR}}.\] Pointwise, \(D_{\mathrm{DR}}x=J_Ax-J_B(R_Ax)\). Thus \(D_{\mathrm{DR}}x=0\) exactly when \(x\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Douglas–Rachford residual is the difference of the two splitting shadows and equals the fixed-point displacement.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Douglas–Rachford operator, displacement, and shadow-difference identity are internally consistent for the stated reflected-resolvent order, but no inspectable splitting reference is supplied.

children.title: Peaceman–Rachford Residuals
children.top_down_role: Residual certificates associated with Peaceman–Rachford fixed-point maps.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x-p)/\gamma\in Ap\), \((p-x)/\gamma\in Bp\), and \(0\in Ap+Bp\); compatible decompositions reconstruct fixed points.

notation.meaning: resolvent shadow of a Peaceman-Rachford fixed point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solution certificate obtained from a zero Peaceman-Rachford residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{Fix}(R_BR_A)\) and \(p=J_{\gamma A}x\), then \((x-p)/\gamma\in Ap\), \((p-x)/\gamma\in Bp\), and \(0\in Ap+Bp\). Conversely, if \(a\in Ap\) and \(-a\in Bp\), then \(x=p+\gamma a\) is a Peaceman-Rachford fixed point with shadow \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Peaceman-Rachford fixed point has a resolvent shadow solving the sum inclusion, and compatible graph decompositions reconstruct fixed points.
knowledge_statements.title: Peaceman-Rachford Shadow Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic geometry of the displacement of the nonexpansive Peaceman-Rachford map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Peaceman-Rachford displacement is \(1/2\)-cocoercive: \(\langle D_{\mathrm{PR}}x-D_{\mathrm{PR}}y,x-y\rangle\ge\tfrac12\|D_{\mathrm{PR}}x-D_{\mathrm{PR}}y\|^2\). In particular, it is monotone and \(2\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Peaceman-Rachford residual is monotone, one-half cocoercive, and two-Lipschitz even though the map need not be averaged.
knowledge_statements.title: Peaceman-Rachford Residual Cocoercivity
Peaceman–Rachford Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Peaceman–Rachford displacement for two maximal monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the reflected-resolvent notation \(R_A=2J_{\gamma A}-I\) and \(R_B=2J_{\gamma B}-I\), the Peaceman–Rachford operator is \(T_{\mathrm{PR}}=R_BR_A\). Its residual is \[D_{\mathrm{PR}}=I-T_{\mathrm{PR}}=I-R_BR_A.\] Therefore \(D_{\mathrm{PR}}x=0\) if and only if \(x\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{PR}}\). With the corresponding Douglas–Rachford residual, one has the exact scaling \(D_{\mathrm{PR}}=2D_{\mathrm{DR}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Peaceman–Rachford residual is the full reflected-resolvent displacement and is twice the corresponding Douglas–Rachford residual.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Peaceman–Rachford residual and its factor-two relation to the corresponding Douglas–Rachford residual are correct under the shared convention, but no source is cited.

assumptions_latex: The unit-relaxation Peaceman-Rachford endpoint is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{PR}}=-I\), so every orbit from \(x_0\ne0\) alternates between \(x_0\) and \(-x_0\).

notation.meaning: normal cone to the singleton origin

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Peaceman-Rachford endpoint can cycle even though the Douglas-Rachford midpoint converges immediately.
knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Relaxation Cycling Boundary

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\lambda=(1-\lambda)I+\lambda T_{\mathrm{PR}}\) is \(\lambda\)-averaged, and its stationary iteration converges weakly to a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Krasnoselskii-Mann convergence for the strict relaxation range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\lambda<1\), \(T_\lambda=(1-\lambda)I+\lambda T_{\mathrm{PR}}\) is \(\lambda\)-averaged. If its fixed-point set is nonempty, \(x_{k+1}=T_\lambda x_k\) is asymptotically regular and converges weakly to a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict relaxation makes the reflected-resolvent map averaged and yields weak fixed-point convergence when fixed points exist.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Relaxation Averagedness and Convergence
Douglas–Rachford-to-Peaceman–Rachford Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation family interpolating identity, Douglas–Rachford, and Peaceman–Rachford maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_{\mathrm{PR}}=R_BR_A\). For \(0<\lambda\leq1\), define the relaxed map \[T_\lambda=(1-\lambda)I+\lambda T_{\mathrm{PR}}.\] Its residual satisfies \[D_\lambda=I-T_\lambda=\lambda(I-T_{\mathrm{PR}})=\lambda D_{\mathrm{PR}}=2\lambda D_{\mathrm{DR}}.\] At \(\lambda=\tfrac12\), \(T_\lambda=T_{\mathrm{DR}}\); at \(\lambda=1\), \(T_\lambda=T_{\mathrm{PR}}\). For every \(\lambda>0\), these maps have the same fixed-point set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxing the Peaceman–Rachford map yields Douglas–Rachford at one-half, while all positive relaxation parameters preserve fixed points and scale residuals linearly.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relaxation representation, endpoint identifications, residual scaling, and fixed-point preservation are consistent on the stated positive parameter range, but no authoritative source is provided.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact stationarity certificate at the intermediate resolvent point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(y=J_{\gamma A}(x-\gamma Bx)\), the FBF displacement satisfies \(R_{\mathrm{FBF},\gamma}(x)/\gamma\in Ay+By\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dividing the FBF residual by the stepsize gives an explicit element of the inclusion operator at the intermediate point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative equivalence of FBF and forward-backward displacements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(R_{\mathrm{FBF},\gamma}(x)=x-y+\gamma(By-Bx)\), \((1-\gamma L)\|x-y\|\le\|R_{\mathrm{FBF},\gamma}(x)\|\le(1+\gamma L)\|x-y\|\). Thus, when \(\gamma L<1\), the FBF residual vanishes exactly when \(x=y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Below the reciprocal Lipschitz stepsize, the FBF residual and the underlying forward-backward displacement are quantitatively equivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: FBF-to-Forward-Backward Residual Equivalence

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration \(x_{k+1}=T_{\mathrm{FBF}}x_k\) converges weakly to a zero of \(A+B\), and \(R_{\mathrm{FBF},\gamma}(x_k)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard constant-stepsize weak-convergence theorem for Tseng splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated assumptions, the iterates \(x_{k+1}=T_{\mathrm{FBF}}x_k\) converge weakly to a point of \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\). Moreover, \(x_k-y_k\to0\) and \(R_{\mathrm{FBF},\gamma}(x_k)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tseng's constant-stepsize FBF iteration converges weakly to a solution and its residual vanishes under the standard monotone-Lipschitz assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Tseng Forward-Backward-Forward Convergence
Forward-Backward-Forward Residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tseng residual for a maximally monotone plus monotone-Lipschitz inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone, let \(B:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz, and let \(0<\gamma<1/L\). For \(x\in\mathcal H\), set \(y=J_{\gamma A}(x-\gamma Bx)\) and \(T_{\mathrm{FBF}}x=y-\gamma(By-Bx)\). The forward-backward-forward residual is
\[
R_{\mathrm{FBF},\gamma}(x)=x-T_{\mathrm{FBF}}x=x-y+\gamma(By-Bx).
\]
It satisfies \(R_{\mathrm{FBF},\gamma}(x)=0\) if and only if \(0\in Ax+Bx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The residual is the displacement produced by Tseng’s forward-backward-forward map, and it vanishes exactly at solutions of the monotone inclusion.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximal monotonicity and resolvent geometry of Spingarn's partial inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The partial inverse \(A_V\) is maximally monotone. Consequently, \(J_{A_V}\) and \(R_{A,V}=I-J_{A_V}\) are firmly nonexpansive. If \(\operatorname{zer}A_V\ne\varnothing\), the iteration \(x_{k+1}=J_{A_V}x_k\) converges weakly to a zero and has summable squared residuals.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Inverse Maximal Monotonicity and Residual Geometry
Partial-Inverse Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent residual of Spingarn’s partial inverse with respect to a closed subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone and let \(V\subset\mathcal H\) be a closed vector subspace. The partial inverse \(A_V\) is defined by
\[
y\in A_Vx\iff P_Vy+P_{V^\perp}x\in A(P_Vx+P_{V^\perp}y).
\]
Its unit-step residual is
\[
R_{A,V}(x)=x-J_{A_V}x=x-P_VJ_Ax-P_{V^\perp}(x-J_Ax).
\]
Consequently, \(R_{A,V}(x)=0\) if and only if \(0\in A_Vx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The partial-inverse residual is the resolvent displacement of Spingarn’s partial inverse and vanishes precisely at its zeros.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is maximally monotone on the real Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\).
\(V\) is a closed vector subspace of \(\mathcal H\).

children.title: Product-Space Residuals

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate Form of the Product-Space Residual Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise form of the diagonal-subspace projections under the standard product inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p_i=J_{A_i}z_i\), \(\bar p=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m p_i\), and \(\bar r=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m(z_i-p_i)\). Then
\[
R_V(\boldsymbol z)=(\bar r,\ldots,\bar r),\qquad R_{V^\perp}(\boldsymbol z)=(p_1-\bar p,\ldots,p_m-\bar p),
\]
and
\[
\|R_V(\boldsymbol z)\|^2=m\|\bar r\|^2,\qquad \|R_{V^\perp}(\boldsymbol z)\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^m\|p_i-\bar p\|^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The balance component is the replicated mean resolvent displacement, while the consensus component contains deviations of the resolvent points from their mean.
assumptions_latex: \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal H}=\mathcal H^m\) carries the standard product inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_V(\boldsymbol z)=(\bar r)_i\quad\text{and}\quad R_{V^\perp}(\boldsymbol z)=(p_i-\bar p)_i.

Product-Space Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal feasibility and balance components induced by a product-space consensus subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\boldsymbol{\mathcal H}=\mathcal H^m\), let \(\boldsymbol A=A_1\times\cdots\times A_m\), and let \(V=\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in\mathcal H\}\). For \(\boldsymbol z\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal H}\), put \(\boldsymbol p=J_{\boldsymbol A}\boldsymbol z\). Define the product-space residual pair by
\[
R_V(\boldsymbol z)=P_V(\boldsymbol z-\boldsymbol p),\qquad R_{V^\perp}(\boldsymbol z)=P_{V^\perp}\boldsymbol p.
\]
The combined residual is \(R_{\mathrm{prod}}(\boldsymbol z)=R_V(\boldsymbol z)+R_{V^\perp}(\boldsymbol z)\). Its vanishing is equivalent to \(\boldsymbol p\in V\) and \(\boldsymbol z-\boldsymbol p\in V^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The product residual combines consensus violation of the resolvent point with the orthogonal balance violation of its resolvent displacement.

\(V\) is the diagonal subspace of \(\mathcal H^m\).

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Inverse-to-Product-Space Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact orthogonal decomposition relating partial-inverse and product-space residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the product-space setting with \(\boldsymbol A=A_1\times\cdots\times A_m\) and diagonal subspace \(V\), the partial-inverse resolvent identity gives
\[
J_{\boldsymbol A_V}\boldsymbol z=P_VJ_{\boldsymbol A}\boldsymbol z+P_{V^\perp}(\boldsymbol z-J_{\boldsymbol A}\boldsymbol z).
\]
Hence
\[
\boldsymbol z-J_{\boldsymbol A_V}\boldsymbol z=P_V(\boldsymbol z-J_{\boldsymbol A}\boldsymbol z)+P_{V^\perp}J_{\boldsymbol A}\boldsymbol z=R_{\mathrm{prod}}(\boldsymbol z).
\]
The two summands are orthogonal, so the squared residual norm equals the sum of their squared norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The partial-inverse residual equals the combined product-space consensus and balance residual, with an orthogonal norm decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is the diagonal subspace of \(\mathcal H^m\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-valued certificate attached to the two Davis-Yin resolvent points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With
\[
x=J_{\gamma B}z,
\qquad
y=J_{\gamma A}(2x-z-\gamma Cx),
\qquad r=x-y,
\]
define
\[
b=\gamma^{-1}(z-x)\in Bx,
\qquad
a=\gamma^{-1}(2x-z-\gamma Cx-y)\in Ay.
\]
Then
\[
a+b+Cx=\gamma^{-1}r.
\]
Thus the splitting residual is exactly \(\gamma\) times a mixed-point graph defect; when \(r=0\), one has \(x=y\) and \(0\in Ax+Bx+Cx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The three-operator residual is an exact scaled inclusion defect with the two set-valued operators evaluated at their respective resolvent points.
knowledge_statements.title: Split Inclusion Defect Identity

assumptions_latex: For the forward-backward reduction, \(C\) is single-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B=0\) yields forward-backward splitting for \(A+C\), while \(C=0\) yields Douglas-Rachford splitting for \(A+B\).

notation.meaning: Zero set-valued operator, whose resolvent is the identity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Principal two-operator specializations of the Davis-Yin residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The three-operator construction contains two canonical two-operator residuals. If \(B=0\), then \(J_{\gamma B}=I\) and
\[
T_\gamma=J_{\gamma A}(I-\gamma C),
\qquad
R_{3,\gamma}=I-J_{\gamma A}(I-\gamma C),
\]
which is the forward-backward fixed-point residual for \(0\in Ax+Cx\). If \(C=0\), then
\[
T_\gamma z=z+J_{\gamma A}(2J_{\gamma B}z-z)-J_{\gamma B}z,
\]
which is the Douglas-Rachford map for \(A+B\), with residual \(J_{\gamma B}z-J_{\gamma A}(2J_{\gamma B}z-z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting one operator reduces the Davis-Yin residual to the standard forward-backward or Douglas-Rachford residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Two-Operator Reductions

notation.meaning: An admissible averagedness constant for the Davis-Yin map.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unrelaxed three-operator iteration in the standard cocoercive step-size regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume \(A,B\) are maximally monotone, \(C\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive, \(0<\gamma<2\beta\), and \(\operatorname{Fix}T_\gamma\neq\varnothing\). Then \(T_\gamma\) is averaged with admissible constant
\[
\alpha=\frac{2\beta}{4\beta-\gamma}\in(0,1).
\]
For \(z_{k+1}=T_\gamma z_k\) and any \(z_*\in\operatorname{Fix}T_\gamma\),
\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|R_{3,\gamma}(z_k)\|^2
\leq\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\|z_0-z_*\|^2.
\]
Consequently \(R_{3,\gamma}(z_k)\to0\), and \(z_k\) converges weakly to a fixed point of \(T_\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the cocoercive step-size range, the Davis-Yin map is averaged; its fixed-point iteration has square-summable residuals and converges weakly when a fixed point exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Davis-Yin Fixed-Point Convergence and Residual Decay
knowledge_statements.title: Davis-Yin Fixed-Point Convergence and Residual Decay
Three-Operator Splitting Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Davis–Yin residual for two maximally monotone operators and one cocoercive operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A,B:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone, let \(C:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be \(\beta\)-cocoercive, and let \(0<\gamma<2\beta\). For \(z\in\mathcal H\), set
\[
x=J_{\gamma B}z,\qquad y=J_{\gamma A}(2x-z-\gamma Cx),\qquad T_\gamma z=z+y-x.
\]
The three-operator splitting residual is \(R_{3,\gamma}(z)=z-T_\gamma z=x-y\). Moreover, \(R_{3,\gamma}(z)=0\) implies that \(x=J_{\gamma B}z\) solves \(0\in Ax+Bx+Cx\), and every solution admits such a fixed-point representative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The three-operator residual is the disagreement of two resolvent points; its zeros encode solutions of the three-operator inclusion.

assumptions_latex: \(p,q\) are produced by the displayed primal-dual resolvent map with \(\tau,0\sigma>0\).

notation.meaning: Graph elements selected by the primal and dual resolvent evaluations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit primal and dual inclusion defects obtained from one primal-dual resolvent evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the seed map, write \(r_x=x-p\) and \(r_v=v-q\). The resolvent relations yield
\[
a:=\tau^{-1}r_x-L^*v\in Ap,
\qquad
b:=\sigma^{-1}r_v+L(2p-x)\in B^{-1}q.
\]
The corresponding Kuhn-Tucker defects at \((p,q)\) satisfy
\[
a+L^*q=\tau^{-1}r_x-L^*r_v,
\qquad
Lp-b=Lr_x-\sigma^{-1}r_v.
\]
In particular,
\[
\|a+L^*q\|\leq\tau^{-1}\|r_x\|+\|L\|\|r_v\|,
\qquad
\|Lp-b\|\leq\|L\|\|r_x\|+\sigma^{-1}\|r_v\|.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal and dual fixed-point displacement components give explicit, norm-controlled Kuhn-Tucker defects.
knowledge_statements.title: Component Residuals Produce Kuhn-Tucker Defects
Primal-Dual Fixed-Point Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual residual for a preconditioned resolvent fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) and \(B:\mathcal G\rightrightarrows\mathcal G\) be maximally monotone, and let \(L:\mathcal H\to\mathcal G\) be bounded linear. For \(\tau,\sigma>0\), define
\[
p=J_{\tau A}(x-\tau L^*v),\qquad q=J_{\sigma B^{-1}}(v+\sigma L(2p-x)).
\]
The primal-dual fixed-point residual is
\[
R_{\mathrm{PD}}(x,v)=(x-p,v-q).
\]
It vanishes if and only if \((x,v)\) satisfies \(-L^*v\in Ax\) and \(Lx\in B^{-1}v\), equivalently \(0\in Ax+L^*v\) and \(v\in B(Lx)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The residual collects primal and dual fixed-point displacements and vanishes exactly at a primal-dual Kuhn–Tucker pair.

children.title: Preconditioned Splitting Residuals
children.top_down_role: Residual certificates under fixed operator preconditioning.

assumptions_latex: \(M\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and satisfies \(M\succeq mI\) for some \(m>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of a fixed-metric forward-backward residual into an ordinary inclusion certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p=T_Mx\), let \(R_M(x)=M(x-p)\), assume \(M\succeq mI\) with \(m>0\), and suppose \(B\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz. The resolvent relation gives
\[
R_M(x)-Bx\in Ap.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{dist}(0,Ap+Bp)
\leq\|R_M(x)+Bp-Bx\|
\leq\left(1+\frac{L}{m}\right)\|R_M(x)\|.
\]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Natural residual of a fixed-metric preconditioned forward-backward map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) be maximally monotone, let \(B:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\), and let \(M:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be bounded, self-adjoint, and strongly positive. Define
\[
T_Mx=J_{M^{-1}A}(x-M^{-1}Bx),\qquad R_M(x)=M(x-T_Mx).
\]
Then \(R_M(x)=0\) if and only if \(0\in Ax+Bx\). If \(p=T_Mx\), the residual also satisfies \(R_M(x)-Bx\in Ap\), so it is directly computable from one preconditioned resolvent evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Metric Splitting Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration-dependent residual generated by a uniformly positive metric sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((M_k)_{k\geq0}\) be bounded, self-adjoint, strongly positive operators on \(\mathcal H\). For the inclusion \(0\in Ax+Bx\), define at iteration \(k\)
\[
T_kx=J_{M_k^{-1}A}(x-M_k^{-1}Bx),\qquad R_k(x)=M_k(x-T_kx).
\]
For every \(k\), \(R_k(x)=0\) if and only if \(0\in Ax+Bx\). If \(mI\preccurlyeq M_k\preccurlyeq MI\) uniformly, then
\[
m\|x-T_kx\|\leq\|R_k(x)\|\leq M\|x-T_kx\|,
\]
so metric-scaled and ordinary fixed-point residuals vanish together uniformly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each iteration uses its current metric, while uniform spectral bounds keep scaled and unscaled residuals quantitatively equivalent.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is maximally monotone and \(B\) is single-valued.
