children.title: Metric-Variation Stability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Comparability and stability limits caused by changing residual metrics.

assumptions_latex: Every \(M_k\) is self-adjoint and positive definite.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of scaled-residual decay when metric norms grow without a common bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Uniform upper spectral control is necessary for an iteration-independent implication from unscaled to scaled residual decay. On \(\mathbb R\), let
\[
M_k=(k+1)I,\qquad r_k=(k+1)^{-1}.
\]
Then \(r_k\to0\), whereas
\[
R_k=M_kr_k=1
\]
for every \(k\). Thus boundedness of each individual \(M_k\), without a common upper bound, does not imply \(r_k\to0\Rightarrow R_k\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metrics growing without a uniform upper bound can keep the scaled residual away from zero even while the underlying displacement vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Uniform Upper Metric Control
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Uniform Upper Metric Control
Metric-Variation Stability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform coercivity is necessary for metric residuals to control ordinary displacements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For metric residuals \(R_k=M_kr_k\), uniform bounds \(mI\preccurlyeq M_k\preccurlyeq MI\) imply \(m\|r_k\|\leq\|R_k\|\leq M\|r_k\|\), hence \(R_k\to0\) if and only if \(r_k\to0\). The lower bound cannot be omitted: on \(\mathcal H=\mathbb R\), take \(M_k=(k+1)^{-1}I\) and \(r_k=1\). Then \(M_k\) is positive definite for every \(k\) and \(R_k=(k+1)^{-1}\to0\), while \(r_k\not\to0\). Thus pointwise positive definiteness alone does not make a metric residual a stable stopping certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a uniform lower spectral bound, metric-scaled residuals may converge to zero while the underlying fixed-point displacement stays nonzero.
assumptions_latex: \(M_k\) is self-adjoint and positive definite for each \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_k\succ0\) pointwise does not imply \(R_k\to0\Rightarrow r_k\to0\); uniform coercivity restores the implication.

knowledge_statements.title: Block Splitting Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal block decomposition of a splitting fixed-point residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal H=\bigoplus_{i=1}^m\mathcal H_i\) be an orthogonal Hilbert direct sum with coordinate projectors \(P_i\), and let \(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) be a splitting fixed-point map. For \(R=I-T\), define the block residuals
\[
R_i(x)=P_iR(x),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.
\]
Then
\[
R(x)=\sum_{i=1}^mR_i(x),\qquad \|R(x)\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^m\|R_i(x)\|^2.
\]
Therefore \(x\in\operatorname{Fix}T\) if and only if every block residual vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthogonal product decomposition splits the global fixed-point residual into block residuals whose squared norms add exactly.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is an orthogonal direct sum of finitely many closed subspaces.
\(T:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H\) is a fixed-point map.

notation.meaning: Orthogonal projector onto coordinate space \(\mathcal H_i\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic aggregation of orthogonal coordinate residual components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal H=\bigoplus_{i=1}^m\mathcal H_i\), let \(P_i\) be the orthogonal coordinate projectors, and set \(R_i=P_iR\). Then
\[
R(x)=\sum_{i=1}^mR_i(x),\qquad \|R(x)\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^m\|R_i(x)\|^2.
\]
Consequently,
\[
R(x)=0\iff R_i(x)=0\ \text{for every }i,
\]
and
\[
\max_i\|R_i(x)\|\leq\|R(x)\|\leq\sqrt m\max_i\|R_i(x)\|.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthogonal coordinate residuals vanish jointly exactly when the full residual vanishes, and their largest norm provides a dimension-calibrated full-residual certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise and Full-Residual Equivalence
Coordinate Splitting Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate residuals and an unbiased single-coordinate residual estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal H=\mathcal H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathcal H_m\), let \(R=I-T\), and write \(R_i=P_iR\). Suppose a random coordinate \(I\) is sampled with probabilities \(p_i>0\). The importance-weighted coordinate residual estimator is
\[
\widehat R(x;I)=p_I^{-1}R_I(x).
\]
Conditionally on \(x\), it satisfies
\[
\mathbb E[\widehat R(x;I)\mid x]=R(x),\qquad
\mathbb E[\|\widehat R(x;I)\|^2\mid x]=\sum_{i=1}^m p_i^{-1}\|R_i(x)\|^2.
\]
Thus one coordinate evaluation provides an unbiased, though generally higher-variance, estimate of the full residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Importance weighting turns one sampled coordinate residual into an unbiased estimator of the complete splitting residual.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is sampled conditionally independently with \(\mathbb P(I=i)=p_i>0\).

children.title: Cross-Block Residual Coupling
children.top_down_role: Coupling, aggregation, and comparability across block or coordinate components.

assumptions_latex: The variable and residual spaces are finite orthogonal block products.
\(L\geq0\) satisfies the displayed componentwise coupling inequalities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of componentwise coupling estimates into a product-space residual bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume
\[
\|R_i(x)-R_i(y)\|\leq\sum_{j=1}^mL_{ij}\|x_j-y_j\|
\]
for a nonnegative matrix \(L\). With \(d_j=\|x_j-y_j\|\) and \(e_i=\|R_i(x)-R_i(y)\|\), one has \(e\leq Ld\) componentwise and therefore
\[
\|R(x)-R(y)\|\leq\|L\|_{2\to2}\|x-y\|.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block coupling matrix supplies a global product-space Lipschitz constant through its induced norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Lipschitz Bound Induced by the Coupling Matrix
knowledge_statements.title: Global Lipschitz Bound Induced by the Coupling Matrix
Cross-Block Residual Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blockwise Lipschitz matrix quantifies how perturbations propagate between residual blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R:\bigoplus_{j=1}^m\mathcal H_j\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^m\mathcal H_i\), with \(R_i=P_iR\). A nonnegative matrix \(L=(L_{ij})\) is a cross-block residual coupling bound if, for all \(x,y\),
\[
\|R_i(x)-R_i(y)\|\leq\sum_{j=1}^mL_{ij}\|x_j-y_j\|,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.
\]
If \(L_{ij}=0\), changing only block \(j\) cannot change residual block \(i\). For an affine residual \(R(x)=Dx+c\), the choice \(L_{ij}=\|P_iDP_j\|\) satisfies the bound and identifies every linear cross-block interaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block Lipschitz matrix records which variable blocks influence each residual block and bounds the strength of those interactions.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a finite orthogonal block product.
\(R_i=P_iR\) is blockwise Lipschitz with finite constants \(L_{ij}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sequence \((\lambda_k)_{k\geq0}\subset(0,1]\), define the sequentially relaxed mappings \[S_k:=(1-\lambda_k)I+\lambda_kT.\] The associated anchored sequential-averaging iteration is \[x^{k+1}:=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)S_kx^k.\] Each \(S_k\) is nonexpansive, and because \(\lambda_k>0\), \(S_kx=x\) holds exactly when \(Tx=x\). children.title: Accelerated Proximal Point via Halpern Iteration

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Yosida Residual Representation of the Resolvent Displacement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent residual and graph realization induced by a maximal-monotone resolvent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximal monotone and \(\lambda>0\). Define \[R_\lambda(x)=x-J_{\lambda A}x,\qquad A_\lambda(x)=\frac1\lambda R_\lambda(x).\] Then \[A_\lambda(x)\in A(J_{\lambda A}x),\qquad x=J_{\lambda A}x+\lambda A_\lambda(x),\] and \[R_\lambda(x)=0\Longleftrightarrow A_\lambda(x)=0\Longleftrightarrow0\in A(x).\] Moreover, \(R_\lambda\) is firmly nonexpansive and \(A_\lambda\) is \(\lambda\)-cocoercive: \[\langle A_\lambda x-A_\lambda y,x-y\rangle\ge\lambda\|A_\lambda x-A_\lambda y\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scaled resolvent displacement is the Yosida approximation; it lies in the operator graph at the resolvent point and has the same zero set.
knowledge_statements.title: Yosida Residual Representation of the Resolvent Displacement
Resolvent Fixed-Point Realization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent representation of zeros of a maximal monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximal monotone, and let \(\lambda>0\). The resolvent \(J_{\lambda A}:=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\) is single-valued, everywhere defined, and firmly nonexpansive. Moreover,
\[
0\in A x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=J_{\lambda A}x,
\]
so \(\operatorname{zer}A=\operatorname{Fix}J_{\lambda A}\). Consequently, applying Halpern iteration to \(J_{\lambda A}\), namely \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)J_{\lambda A}x_k\), realizes the monotone inclusion as an anchored fixed-point problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zeros of a maximal monotone operator are exactly fixed points of its firmly nonexpansive resolvent, so Halpern iteration can solve the inclusion through resolvent evaluations.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically standard, matches the fixed-point-realization leaf, and representation is the appropriate content kind. However, the record contains no citation, locator, or inspectable evidence for the resolvent properties and zero/fixed-point equivalence, so source support is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural realization of the resolvent displacement for a maximal monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximal monotone and \(\lambda>0\). Its Yosida approximation is \[A_\lambda:=\lambda^{-1}(I-J_{\lambda A}).\] Then \(A_\lambda x\in A(J_{\lambda A}x)\), \(A_\lambda x=0\iff0\in Ax\), and \(A_\lambda\) is \(\lambda\)-cocoercive: \[\langle A_\lambda x-A_\lambda y,x-y\rangle\geq\lambda\|A_\lambda x-A_\lambda y\|^2.\] In particular, \(A_\lambda\) is single-valued, monotone, and \(1/\lambda\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scaled resolvent displacement is the Yosida approximation, an explicit Lipschitz monotone residual with the same zero set as the inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Yosida Approximation as the Scaled Inclusion Residual
knowledge_statements.title: Yosida Approximation as the Scaled Inclusion Residual
Monotone-Inclusion Residual Realization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent residual for a maximal monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximal monotone and \(\lambda>0\). Define \(p=J_{\lambda A}x\) and the fixed-point residual \(R_\lambda x=x-J_{\lambda A}x\). The resolvent identity gives
\[
\frac{1}{\lambda}R_\lambda x\in A p.
\]
Hence \(R_\lambda x=0\) if and only if \(0\in A x\). More generally, \(\|R_\lambda x\|/\lambda\) is the norm of an explicitly available inclusion residual at the resolvent point \(p\), rather than necessarily at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent displacement produces an explicit graph element of the operator and vanishes exactly at solutions of the monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda^{-1}R_\lambda x\in A(J_{\lambda A}x)\) and \(R_\lambda x=0\iff 0\in Ax\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The resolvent identity and its distinction between the evaluation point x and resolvent point p are precise, and representation fits the leaf. Parameter-Free Halpern Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical Halpern schedule requiring no problem-dependent tuning constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a Hilbert space \(H\), a nonexpansive map \(T:H\to H\), an anchor \(u\in H\), and \(x_0\in H\), set
\[
\alpha_k=\frac{1}{k+2},\qquad x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)Tx_k,
\qquad k=0,1,\ldots .
\]
Stop when a prescribed test such as \(\|x_k-Tx_k\|\leq\varepsilon\) holds, and output \(x_k\). The schedule is parameter-free in the sense that it uses neither a Lipschitz constant nor a strong-monotonicity modulus; the tolerance \(\varepsilon\) only specifies termination.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(T:H\to H\) is nonexpansive.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y_k\) satisfy \(\|y_k-Tx_k\|\leq\varepsilon_k\). Then \[\bigl|\|x_k-y_k\|-\|x_k-Tx_k\|\bigr|\leq\varepsilon_k,\] and therefore \[\max\{0,\|x_k-y_k\|-\varepsilon_k\}\leq\|x_k-Tx_k\|\leq\|x_k-y_k\|+\varepsilon_k.\] Thus the computable test \(\|x_k-y_k\|+\varepsilon_k\leq\varepsilon\) certifies \(\|x_k-Tx_k\|\leq\varepsilon\).

Inexact-Resolvent Halpern Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Halpern iteration with certified additive resolvent errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T=J_{\lambda A}\), where \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone. Given \(u,x_0\in H\), weights \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\), and error budgets \(\varepsilon_k\geq0\), compute \(y_k\) satisfying \(\|y_k-Tx_k\|\leq\varepsilon_k\), and update
\[
x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)y_k.
\]
Stop when both \(\|x_k-y_k\|\leq\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon_k\leq\varepsilon\) hold, and output \(x_k\). Equivalently, \(y_k=Tx_k+e_k\) with \(\|e_k\|\leq\varepsilon_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace each exact resolvent evaluation in Halpern iteration by a point with a certified additive error and monitor both displacement and oracle error.

children.title: Parameter-Free Robustness to Resolvent Error
children.top_down_role: Interaction between parameter-free design and resolvent inexactness.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Free Robustness to Resolvent Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic perturbation bound for the universal Halpern schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:H\to H\) be nonexpansive. From the same \(x_0\) and anchor \(u\), let \(\bar x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)T\bar x_k\) and \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)(Tx_k+e_k)\), where \(\alpha_k=1/(k+2)\) and \(\|e_k\|\leq\varepsilon_k\). Then, for every \(N\geq1\),
\[
\|x_N-\bar x_N\|\leq\frac{1}{N+1}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(k+1)\varepsilon_k.
\]
Thus convergence of the inexact trajectory to the exact one follows whenever the displayed weighted error average tends to zero, without using a problem-dependent constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the universal Halpern weights, accumulated resolvent error is controlled by an explicit weighted average that contains no problem-dependent tuning parameter.
assumptions_latex: The exact and inexact sequences share \(x_0\) and \(u\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Property is the appropriate content kind, and the displayed weighted perturbation bound is consistent with the stated universal Halpern weights. Because this is a nontrivial quantitative claim and no source or locator is supplied, authoritative support is required.

children.title: Halpern Forward-Backward Splitting
children.top_down_role: Halpern anchoring applied to forward-backward fixed-point maps.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-iterate inclusion certificate at the forward-backward point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(y=J_{\gamma A}(x-\gamma Bx)\), define \(v=(x-y)/\gamma+By-Bx\). Then \(v\in Ay+By\) and \(\|v\|\leq(\gamma^{-1}+\beta^{-1})\|x-y\|\). Thus the fixed-point displacement gives a computable graph-residual certificate at \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One forward-backward displacement constructs an explicit residual in Ay+By whose norm is controlled by the displacement.
knowledge_statements.title: Forward-Backward Graph Residual Certificate

assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone and \(B:H\to H\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive.

notation.meaning: metric projection onto the solution set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong convergence of Halpern anchoring applied to a cocoercive forward-backward map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(T=J_{\gamma A}(I-\gamma B)\) and \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)Tx_k\). Under the stated assumptions, \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\), \(x_k\to P_{\operatorname{zer}(A+B)}u\) strongly, and \(\|x_k-Tx_k\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With standard Halpern weights, anchored forward-backward iterates converge strongly to the solution nearest the anchor and their fixed-point residual vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Convergence of Halpern Forward-Backward Iterates
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Convergence of Halpern Forward-Backward Iterates
Halpern Forward-Backward Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Anchored forward-backward iteration for a cocoercive-plus-maximal-monotone inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximal monotone and let \(B:H\to H\) be \(\beta\)-cocoercive. Choose \(\gamma\in(0,2\beta)\), an anchor \(u\in H\), and weights \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\). Define the forward-backward map \(T_{\mathrm{FB}}=J_{\gamma A}(I-\gamma B)\) and iterate
\[
y_k=J_{\gamma A}(x_k-\gamma Bx_k),\qquad
x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)y_k.
\]
Stop when \(\|x_k-y_k\|\leq\varepsilon\), and output \(x_k\). Its fixed points satisfy \(0\in Ax+Bx\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply one forward step for the cocoercive operator, one backward resolvent step, then anchor the resulting fixed-point iteration.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is maximal monotone and \(B\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive on a real Hilbert space.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The forward-backward map, step-size range, and fixed-point characterization match the leaf, and algorithm is the correct kind. No citation supports the Halpern variant, and the residual stopping rule is presented without a source establishing what accuracy it certifies.

children.title: Halpern Douglas–Rachford Splitting
children.top_down_role: Halpern anchoring applied to Douglas–Rachford fixed-point maps.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-iterate graph certificate furnished by one Douglas-Rachford resolvent sweep.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p=J_{\gamma B}x\) and \(q=J_{\gamma A}(2p-x)\), the resolvent relations give \((x-p)/\gamma\in Bp\), \((2p-x-q)/\gamma\in Aq\), and hence \((p-q)/\gamma\in Aq+Bp\). Therefore \(\|p-q\|/\gamma\) is a computable split graph residual, and \(p=q\) implies \(p\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The displacement between the two resolvent points produces an explicit element of the split inclusion Aq+Bp; zero displacement makes the shadow an exact solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Douglas-Rachford Split Residual Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong convergence of Halpern anchoring applied to the Douglas-Rachford fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=\tfrac12(I+R_{\gamma A}R_{\gamma B})\). If \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)Tx_k\), then under the stated assumptions \(x_k\to P_{\operatorname{Fix}T}u\) strongly, \(\|x_k-Tx_k\|\to0\), and the shadows \(J_{\gamma B}x_k\) converge strongly to \(J_{\gamma B}P_{\operatorname{Fix}T}u\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard Halpern weights make the Douglas-Rachford fixed-point iterates converge strongly to the fixed point nearest the anchor, while their resolvent shadows converge to an inclusion solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Convergence of Halpern Douglas-Rachford Iterates
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Convergence of Halpern Douglas-Rachford Iterates
Halpern Douglas–Rachford Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Anchored Douglas–Rachford iteration for two maximal monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximal monotone, choose \(\gamma>0\), an anchor \(u\in H\), and weights \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\). Define
\[
p_k=J_{\gamma B}x_k,
\qquad q_k=J_{\gamma A}(2p_k-x_k),
\qquad z_k=x_k+q_k-p_k,
\]
then update \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)z_k\). Stop when \(\|q_k-p_k\|\leq\varepsilon\), and output the shadow point \(p_k\). Whenever \(x_k\) is a fixed point of the Douglas–Rachford map, \(p_k\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perform the two resolvent evaluations of Douglas–Rachford splitting, anchor its fixed-point update, and return the resolvent shadow as the inclusion solution.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed Douglas-Rachford sweep and conditional shadow fixed-point statement are standard, and algorithm fits the leaf. A source is still required; additionally, any convergence or eventual-output interpretation would require a nonempty solution/fixed-point assumption and justified Halpern weights, neither of which is stated or cited.

children.title: Halpern Splitting Applicability Contrast
children.top_down_role: Operator regimes distinguishing the two anchored splitting families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical obstruction separating the explicit forward-backward regime from the two-resolvent regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(H=\mathbb R^2\), let \(S(x_1,x_2)=(-x_2,x_1)\) and \(A=0\). The operator \(S\) is monotone, \(1\)-Lipschitz, and maximal monotone, but it is not \(\beta\)-cocoercive for any \(\beta>0\). For every \(\gamma>0\), the forward-backward map \(I-\gamma S\) has norm \(\sqrt{1+\gamma^2}>1\), whereas the resolvents required by Douglas-Rachford remain everywhere defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A skew rotation is monotone and Lipschitz but not cocoercive; its explicit forward step expands, while the maximal-monotone resolvent regime remains available.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone Lipschitzness Does Not Suffice for Forward-Backward Splitting
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Lipschitzness Does Not Suffice for Forward-Backward Splitting
Halpern Splitting Applicability Contrast
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator assumptions distinguishing forward-backward and Douglas–Rachford Halpern schemes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the inclusion \(0\in Ax+Bx\) on a real Hilbert space, the Halpern forward-backward realization applies when \(A\) is maximal monotone, \(B\) is single-valued and \(\beta\)-cocoercive, and \(0<\gamma<2\beta\). The Halpern Douglas–Rachford realization instead applies when both \(A\) and \(B\) are maximal monotone and their resolvents can be evaluated, with arbitrary \(\gamma>0\). Thus Douglas–Rachford permits both terms to be set-valued, whereas forward-backward replaces one resolvent by an explicit evaluation but requires cocoercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward-backward needs one cocoercive explicit operator; Douglas–Rachford accommodates two maximal monotone operators but requires both resolvents.
assumptions_latex: The target problem is \(0\in Ax+Bx\) on a real Hilbert space.
The required operator evaluations or resolvents are computationally available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{FB: }A\text{ maximal monotone},\ B\text{ cocoercive};\qquad \text{DR: }A,B\text{ maximal monotone}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is the correct role for this applicability-contrast leaf, and the forward-backward versus Douglas-Rachford assumptions are stated consistently. The comparison is nontrivial and has no specific supporting citation or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Anchored Extragradient Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-evaluation anchored extragradient scheme for a monotone Lipschitz operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space and let \(F:C\to H\) be monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz. Given \(u,x_0\in C\), choose \(\eta_k>0\) and \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\), and compute
\[
y_k=P_C(x_k-\eta_kF(x_k)),
\qquad
z_k=P_C(x_k-\eta_kF(y_k)),
\qquad
x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)z_k.
\]
Stop when \(\|x_k-y_k\|\leq\varepsilon\), and output \(x_k\). The two evaluations distinguish the method from a single forward projected step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Take a projected prediction, evaluate the operator there, form a projected correction, and average that correction with a fixed anchor.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits the leaf, but arbitrary positive step sizes are insufficient for the usual convergence theory of monotone Lipschitz extragradient methods. The particular anchored two-projection variant, admissible step-size conditions, anchor schedule, and meaning of the stopping test require a specific source before a reliable mathematical record can be fixed.

children.title: Halpern-Type Primal-Dual Variants
children.top_down_role: Anchored variants built from primal-dual fixed-point maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Halpern-Type Primal-Dual Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Halpern anchoring of a primal-dual proximal fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min_x f(x)+g(Kx)\), where \(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions and \(K\) is bounded linear. Given \(w_k=(x_k,y_k)\), form
\[
\widehat x_k=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}(x_k-\tau K^*y_k),
\qquad
\widehat y_k=\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma g^*}\bigl(y_k+\sigma K(2\widehat x_k-x_k)\bigr),
\]
and set \(w_{k+1}=\alpha_k w_0+(1-\alpha_k)(\widehat x_k,\widehat y_k)\). Choose \(\tau\sigma\|K\|^2<1\). Stop when \(\|w_k-(\widehat x_k,\widehat y_k)\|\leq\varepsilon\), and output \(w_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply a standard primal-dual proximal step and anchor the resulting product-space fixed-point iteration at the initial primal-dual pair.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is appropriate for the variant leaf, but the primal and dual Hilbert spaces and domains of f, g, and K are not introduced. Moreover, applying Halpern iteration requires the metric in which the displayed primal-dual map is nonexpansive or averaged; the Euclidean-looking product residual is not justified. A variant-specific source is needed to determine the correct formulation.

children.title: Halpern-Type ADMM Variants
children.top_down_role: Anchored variants built from ADMM fixed-point realizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Halpern-Type ADMM Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Anchored ADMM fixed-point iteration for a linearly constrained convex problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min_{x,z} f(x)+g(z)\) subject to \(Ax+Bz=c\), with penalty \(\rho>0\). From \(w_k=(x_k,z_k,y_k)\), compute the standard scaled ADMM map \(\widehat w_k=T_{\mathrm{ADMM}}w_k\) by
\[
\widehat x_k\in\arg\min_x f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|Ax+Bz_k-c+y_k\|^2,
\]
\[
\widehat z_k\in\arg\min_z g(z)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|A\widehat x_k+Bz-c+y_k\|^2,
\qquad
\widehat y_k=y_k+A\widehat x_k+B\widehat z_k-c.
\]
Then set \(w_{k+1}=\alpha_k w_0+(1-\alpha_k)\widehat w_k\) and stop when the fixed-point residual is below tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute one scaled ADMM sweep, then average the complete primal-dual state with a fixed anchor using Halpern weights.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
The displayed ADMM subproblems attain selected minimizers.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the intended content kind, but selected minimizers need not define a single-valued full-state ADMM map, and standard ADMM is not automatically a nonexpansive self-map on the displayed (x,z,y) state in the ordinary product norm. The fixed-point residual used for termination is also not specified. A concrete anchored-ADMM source is necessary to fix these choices.

children.title: Primal-Dual-to-ADMM Residual Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Residual translation and equivalence boundaries across the two variant families.

assumptions_latex: \(M:W\to V\) intertwines two fixed-point maps but is not assumed injective.

notation.meaning: fixed-point maps on the two state spaces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for transporting fixed-point residuals between two state-space realizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W=\mathbb R^2\), \(V=\mathbb R\), \(M(a,b)=a\), \(T_W(a,b)=(a,0)\), and \(T_V=I_V\). Then \(T_VM=MT_W\), but \((I-T_V)Mw=0\) for every \(w\), whereas \((I-T_W)(a,b)=(0,b)\). Thus noninjective intertwining can erase residual components and cannot yield two-sided residual equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A noninjective state transformation can erase residual components, so intertwining alone gives only one-way transport and not residual equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Noninvertible Intertwining Does Not Give Residual Equivalence
knowledge_statements.title: Noninvertible Intertwining Does Not Give Residual Equivalence
Primal-Dual-to-ADMM Residual Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual transport under a primal-dual/ADMM fixed-point conjugacy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T_{\mathrm{PD}}:W\to W\) and \(T_{\mathrm{ADMM}}:V\to V\) be primal-dual and ADMM fixed-point maps for the same convex problem. Suppose an invertible bounded linear change of variables \(M:W\to V\) satisfies \(T_{\mathrm{ADMM}}=MT_{\mathrm{PD}}M^{-1}\). Then, for \(v=Mw\),
\[
v-T_{\mathrm{ADMM}}v=M(w-T_{\mathrm{PD}}w).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\|M^{-1}\|^{-1}\|w-T_{\mathrm{PD}}w\|
\leq \|v-T_{\mathrm{ADMM}}v\|
\leq \|M\|\|w-T_{\mathrm{PD}}w\|.
\]
Thus the two residuals vanish simultaneously and are quantitatively equivalent under a well-conditioned correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When primal-dual and ADMM maps are conjugate, their fixed-point residuals are related by the same variable transformation and vanish simultaneously.
assumptions_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{PD}}\) and \(T_{\mathrm{ADMM}}\) describe the same problem under a change of variables.
\(M\) is bounded, linear, invertible, and intertwines the two maps.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic residual transport is correct under the assumed bounded linear conjugacy, and representation is the appropriate kind. However, the record merely assumes the substantive primal-dual-to-ADMM correspondence instead of identifying concrete maps and a transformation for a specified problem. No source supports that leaf-specific conjugacy, so the mathematical specialization remains unreliable.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Tight residual rate and performance-estimation analysis
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: On the Convergence Rate of the Halpern-Iteration

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(T:H\to H\) is nonexpansive with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x_k-Tx_k\|=\Theta(R/(k+1))\) in the worst case over the stated class.

notation.meaning: Scale relative to the fixed-point set

review_flags: Exact universal constants and the matching worst-case construction require an authoritative Halpern-rate source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case deterministic Halpern residual rate for general nonexpansive fixed-point maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) such that, for every admissible instance and every \(k\ge 0\), \[\|x_k-Tx_k\|\le \frac{CR}{k+1}.\] Conversely, for every \(k\), some Hilbert space, nonexpansive map, anchor, and initial point satisfying the assumptions obey \[\|x_k-Tx_k\|\ge \frac{cR}{k+1}.\] Thus the last-iterate fixed-point residual order \(1/(k+1)\) is unimprovable uniformly over this class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Halpern iteration attains a worst-case last-iterate fixed-point residual proportional to 1/k, and matching instances prevent a uniformly faster rate.
knowledge_statements.title: Tight Nonexpansive Residual Rates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits this terminal container, and the upper/lower formulation is locally appropriate. However, the matching worst-case lower bound, its quantifiers, and the normalization by R require a primary Halpern residual-complexity source with a precise theorem locator.

assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space, \(\gamma>0\), and \(\operatorname{zer}A\ne\varnothing\).
\(T=J_{\gamma A}=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}\), and \((x_k)\) is the Halpern sequence for \(T\) with weights \(1/(k+2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(y_k=J_{\gamma A}x_k\), a last-iterate inclusion residual satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(0,Ay_k)=O(1/(\gamma(k+1)))\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent point associated with the iterate

review_flags: The inherited Halpern residual constant requires source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent reduction of a maximal-monotone inclusion to a nonexpansive fixed-point residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(x_k-y_k\in\gamma Ay_k\), one has \[\operatorname{dist}(0,Ay_k)\le \frac{\|x_k-y_k\|}{\gamma}=\frac{\|x_k-Tx_k\|}{\gamma}.\] Hence any bound \(\|x_k-Tx_k\|\le CR/(k+1)\) yields the last-iterate estimate \[\operatorname{dist}(0,Ay_k)\le \frac{CR}{\gamma(k+1)}.\] Consequently, \(k=O(CR/(\gamma\varepsilon))\) iterations suffice to produce \(y_k\) with \(\operatorname{dist}(0,Ay_k)\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying Halpern iteration to a resolvent converts its 1/k fixed-point residual directly into a 1/k last-iterate monotone-inclusion residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Last-Iterate Monotone-Inclusion Rates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The resolvent residual conversion is mathematically standard, but the stated O(1/k) estimate inherits an unsourced Halpern rate and constant. The statement also includes derivational proof text. An authoritative locator is needed before selecting a reliable complete replacement.

children.title: Near-Optimal Residual Complexity
children.top_down_role: Residual complexity guarantees approaching known performance limits.

assumptions_latex: For residual tolerance \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), an algorithm has upper complexity \(U(\varepsilon)\le C\varepsilon^{-1}(1+\log(1/\varepsilon))^q\) for some \(q\ge0\).
Every algorithm in the same oracle model has worst-case complexity \(L(\varepsilon)\ge c\varepsilon^{-1}\), with \(c,C>0\) independent of \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm is optimal up to the factor \((C/c)(1+\log(1/\varepsilon))^q\).
review_flags: This is a conditional complexity classification; instantiation for a particular Halpern oracle model requires sources.
standard_field_rationale: near-optimality is conventionally measured by the upper-to-lower complexity ratio.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional definition of near-optimality relative to a fixed residual oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The upper-to-lower ratio satisfies \[1\le \frac{U(\varepsilon)}{L(\varepsilon)}\le \frac{C}{c}\bigl(1+\log(1/\varepsilon)\bigr)^q.\] Therefore the method is near-optimal in residual oracle complexity: it matches the minimax algebraic dependence \(\varepsilon^{-1}\), with at most a polylogarithmic loss. When \(q=0\), the upper and lower bounds agree up to constants and the method is order-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper bound matching the minimax 1/epsilon lower bound up to logarithmic factors is near-optimal; with no logarithm it is order-optimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Near-Optimal Residual Complexity

children.title: Residual Complexity Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Oracle and problem-class limitations on achievable residual complexity.

assumptions_latex: A deterministic algorithm accesses an unknown nonexpansive map only through adaptive evaluations \(Tx_0,\ldots,Tx_{N-1}\).
The admissible class permits Hilbert-space dimension depending on \(N\), has a fixed point, and is normalized by \(\inf_{z\in\operatorname{Fix}T}\|x_0-z\|\le R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimax fixed-point residual after \(N\) oracle calls is bounded below by \(cR/(N+1)\) for a universal \(c>0\).
review_flags: The exact black-box model, dimension requirement, and lower-bound constant need a primary complexity source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax deterministic value-oracle lower bound for nonexpansive fixed-point residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There is a universal constant \(c>0\) such that, for every \(N\ge1\) and every deterministic adaptive algorithm in the stated oracle model, an admissible instance exists for which the algorithm's output \(\widehat x_N\) satisfies \[\|\widehat x_N-T\widehat x_N\|\ge \frac{cR}{N+1}.\] Equivalently, guaranteeing \(\|\widehat x_N-T\widehat x_N\|\le\varepsilon\) uniformly requires \(N=\Omega(R/\varepsilon)\) oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: No deterministic black-box method can uniformly obtain nonexpansive residual epsilon using asymptotically fewer than R/epsilon operator evaluations.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Complexity Lower Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a substantive minimax lower-bound theorem. Its validity depends on the exact deterministic oracle model, allowable output rule, dimension growth, normalization, and resisting-oracle construction, none of which has cited support.

children.title: Upper-to-Lower Complexity Gap
children.top_down_role: Remaining separations between attainable guarantees and lower bounds.

assumptions_latex: \(U(\varepsilon)\) is a valid worst-case upper oracle bound and \(L(\varepsilon)>0\) is a valid minimax lower bound for the same instance class, oracle, output rule, and residual criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The multiplicative gap is \(G(\varepsilon)=U(\varepsilon)/L(\varepsilon)\), and comparison is meaningful only under a common model.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: complexity gaps are ratios only after aligning the oracle and accuracy conventions.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-aligned metric for the unresolved gap between residual upper and lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[G(\varepsilon):=\frac{U(\varepsilon)}{L(\varepsilon)}.\] Constant \(G(\varepsilon)\) means order-optimal complexity, polylogarithmic \(G(\varepsilon)\) means near-optimal complexity, and polynomially divergent \(G(\varepsilon)\) identifies an algebraic gap. If the bounds use different oracle access, randomization, dimensions, success probabilities, or residual notions, their ratio is not an upper-to-lower complexity gap until those conventions are aligned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complexity gap is the upper bound divided by the lower bound, provided both use exactly the same oracle, instance class, and accuracy criterion.
knowledge_statements.title: Upper-to-Lower Complexity Gap

children.title: Stochastic Halpern Complexity
children.top_down_role: Residual complexity under stochastic oracle access.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected Fixed-Point Residual Does Not Certify a Realized Tolerance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rare-event boundary separating expected stochastic residual control from realized residual certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(T(x)=0\). For \(a>0\) and \(p\in(0,1)\), let a stochastic method return \(X=a/p\) with probability \(p\) and \(X=0\) otherwise. Its fixed-point residual \(Z=|X-TX|\) satisfies \[\mathbb E Z=a,\qquad \mathbb P(Z>a)=p.\] Thus an expected-residual bound alone permits arbitrarily large residuals on rare events and does not certify the realized output at the same tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small expected fixed-point residual can hide an arbitrarily large rare-event residual and is not a realized stopping certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Expected Fixed-Point Residual Does Not Certify a Realized Tolerance

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Markov High-Probability Conversion of an Expected Halpern Residual Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tail conversion from the conditional bias-plus-sampling expected-residual estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z=\|X_K-TX_K\|\ge0\) and suppose \[\mathbb EZ\le\frac{C_1R}{K+1}+\frac{C_2\sigma}{\sqrt M}.\] For \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\delta\in(0,1)\), the choices \[K+1\ge\frac{2C_1R}{\delta\varepsilon},\qquad M\ge\frac{4C_2^2\sigma^2}{\delta^2\varepsilon^2}\] imply \(\mathbb P(Z>\varepsilon)\le\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Markov's inequality converts the conditional expected-residual estimate into a loose high-probability bound.
assumptions_latex: The nonnegative residual satisfies the displayed expected-value estimate.
knowledge_statements.title: Markov High-Probability Conversion of an Expected Halpern Residual Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic Halpern recursion and unbiased oracle model without an algorithm-specific convergence claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\to H\), let \(u,x_0\in H\), and let \((\mathcal F_k)\) be a filtration. At iteration \(k\), draw \(b_k\ge1\) conditionally independent samples \(\mathcal T(x_k,\xi_{k,j})\), define \[\widehat T_kx_k=\frac1{b_k}\sum_{j=1}^{b_k}\mathcal T(x_k,\xi_{k,j}),\] and update \[x_{k+1}=\alpha_{k+1}u+(1-\alpha_{k+1})\widehat T_kx_k,\qquad 0<\alpha_{k+1}\le1.\] If \[\mathbb E[\mathcal T(x_k,\xi_{k,j})\mid\mathcal F_k]=Tx_k,\qquad \mathbb E[\|\mathcal T(x_k,\xi_{k,j})-Tx_k\|^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le\sigma^2,\] then \(\mathbb E[\widehat T_kx_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=Tx_k\) and \(\mathbb E[\|\widehat T_kx_k-Tx_k\|^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le\sigma^2/b_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic Halpern step averages unbiased operator samples and combines the estimate with a fixed anchor using the Halpern weight.
assumptions_latex: Within each batch, samples are conditionally independent and unbiased with conditional variance at most \(\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minibatch estimate is conditionally unbiased with mean-square error at most \(\sigma^2/b_k\), and the update defines a filtration-adapted stochastic Halpern recursion.
knowledge_statements.title: Filtration-Adapted Minibatch Stochastic Halpern Recursion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact accounting of stochastic-operator work for a declared batch schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K\) stochastic Halpern iterations with batch sizes \(b_0,\ldots,b_{K-1}\), the number of stochastic-operator samples is \[M_K=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}b_k.\] If \(b_k=b\), then \(M_K=Kb\). Consequently, a bound involving an aggregate \(M\) is not a total oracle bound until its allocation across iterations is specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total stochastic-oracle work is the sum of the iterationwise batch sizes.
assumptions_latex: Iteration \(k\) evaluates exactly \(b_k\) stochastic operator samples.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_K=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}b_k\), and \(M_K=Kb\) for a uniform batch size.

notation.meaning: total stochastic-operator calls through K iterations

knowledge_statements.title: Iterationwise Batch Accounting

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Persistent Residual Noise Under Unit Batching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of stochastic Halpern residual convergence under unbiased fixed-variance samples without batch growth or variance reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\mathbb R\), \(T(x)=0\), \(u=0\), and let the oracle return independent samples \(\mathcal T(x,\xi_k)=\xi_k\), where \(\mathbb P(\xi_k=\sigma)=\mathbb P(\xi_k=-\sigma)=1/2\) and \(\sigma>0\). With unit batches, \[x_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_{k+1})\xi_k,\qquad \mathbb E|x_{k+1}-Tx_{k+1}|=(1-\alpha_{k+1})\sigma.\] Hence \(\alpha_k\to0\) implies \(\mathbb E|x_k-Tx_k|\to\sigma\), not zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Persistent unbiased oracle noise prevents residual convergence with unit batches when the Halpern anchor weights vanish.
assumptions_latex: Oracle samples are independent Rademacher variables of magnitude \(\sigma>0\).
Every iteration uses one sample and \(0<\alpha_k\le1\).
knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Residual Noise Under Unit Batching

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(T:H\to H\), \(R\ge 0\), \(\sigma\ge 0\), and \(C_1,C_2>0\).
A stochastic procedure returns an \(H\)-valued random variable \(X_K\) after \(K\ge 0\) iterations using \(M\ge 1\) samples and satisfies \(\mathbb E\|X_K-TX_K\|\le C_1R/(K+1)+C_2\sigma/\sqrt M\).
The samples are unbiased and satisfy the second-moment assumptions represented by the noise scale \(\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Expected residual at most \(\varepsilon\) is guaranteed by \(K+1\ge 2C_1R/\varepsilon\) and \(M\ge 4C_2^2\sigma^2/\varepsilon^2\).
review_flags: Conditional complexity statement; a concrete stochastic algorithm and authoritative source are required for algorithm-specific promotion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional expected-residual sample and iteration complexity under a bias-plus-sampling-error estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), the choices \[K+1\ge \frac{2C_1R}{\varepsilon}\qquad\text{and}\qquad M\ge \frac{4C_2^2\sigma^2}{\varepsilon^2}\] guarantee \[\mathbb E\|X_K-TX_K\|\le \varepsilon.\] Thus the conditional iteration complexity is \(O(R/\varepsilon)\), and the conditional stochastic-oracle complexity is \(O(\sigma^2/\varepsilon^2)\). This conclusion is in expectation; it does not provide a high-probability guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the assumed deterministic 1/K term and sampling 1/sqrt(M) term, expected residual epsilon requires order R/epsilon iterations and sigma-squared/epsilon-squared samples. No high-probability claim is made.
knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Halpern Complexity

children.title: Finite-Sum Halpern Complexity
children.top_down_role: Residual complexity exploiting finite-sum problem structure.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(n\ge 1\), and \(T_i:H\to H\) for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
The averaged map \(T:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nT_i\) is nonexpansive, and evaluating one component \(T_i x\) costs one component-oracle call.
For constants \(C>0\) and \(R\\ge 0\), a full-evaluation Halpern method satisfies \(\|x_K-Tx_K\|\le CR/(K+1)\) for every \(K\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The full-batch component-oracle complexity for residual tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) is \(O(nR/\varepsilon)\).
review_flags: Full-batch baseline only; no optimal finite-sum complexity is asserted.
The assumed Halpern residual rate requires an authoritative source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-batch component-oracle baseline for a finite-sum nonexpansive operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), taking \[K+1\ge \frac{CR}{\varepsilon}\] guarantees \[\|x_K-Tx_K\|\le \varepsilon.\] Since each full evaluation of \(T\) uses \(n\) component evaluations, the resulting component-oracle complexity is \[nK=O\!\left(\frac{nR}{\varepsilon}\right).\] This is a full-batch baseline and not an optimality claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluating all n components at every Halpern step gives a full-batch component-oracle baseline of order nR/epsilon. The statement does not claim this dependence is optimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Halpern Complexity

children.title: Stochastic-to-Finite-Sum Oracle Separation
children.top_down_role: Complexity distinctions across stochastic and component-access regimes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gaussian Mean Instance Separates Fresh Samples from Finite Indexed Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative information separation using the same constant-map fixed-point residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mu\in\mathbb R\), let \(T_\mu(x)=\mu\), so \(\operatorname{Fix}T_\mu=\{\mu\}\) and \(\|x-T_\mu x\|=|x-\mu|\). In an indexed finite-sum realization \(\mu=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\), querying all \(n\) components computes a zero-residual point exactly. Under fresh sampling, suppose each query returns \(Y\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\). Any estimator \(\widehat x\) satisfying \(\mathbb P_\mu(|\widehat x-\mu|<\varepsilon)\ge2/3\) for both \(\mu=-2\varepsilon\) and \(\mu=2\varepsilon\) requires \[m\ge\frac{\sigma^2}{36\varepsilon^2}.\] Hence the two oracle complexities cannot be converted by substituting dataset size for variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The constant-map residual can be solved exactly after one finite pass, while fresh Gaussian sampling requires order sigma squared over epsilon squared observations for constant success probability.
assumptions_latex: The indexed oracle returns selected fixed components \(a_i\).
The stochastic oracle returns independent \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) samples.
The success requirement holds for both \(\mu=\pm2\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: m\ge\frac{\sigma^2}{36\varepsilon^2}\text{ for fresh samples, whereas }n\text{ indexed calls recover }\mu\text{ exactly}.

notation.meaning: constant nonexpansive operator with fixed point mu

knowledge_statements.title: Gaussian Mean Instance Separates Fresh Samples from Finite Indexed Access

assumptions_latex: In the online stochastic model, an algorithm receives independent unbiased samples of an operator, with noise represented by a variance scale \(\sigma^2>0\).
In the finite-sum model, an algorithm has indexed access to a fixed collection \(T_1,\ldots,T_n\), so components may be revisited and their evaluations reused.
Complexities are compared for the same residual criterion and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Online stochastic sample complexity and indexed finite-sum component complexity are not interchangeable without an explicit reduction between their oracle models.

notation.meaning: Noise scale in the online stochastic model

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fresh-sample and indexed finite-sum oracles expose different reusable information.
A quantitative separation requires specified oracle models and matching lower bounds.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information boundary between fresh-sample and reusable indexed-component oracle models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An indexed finite-sum oracle permits repeated access to a selected component, reuse of stored component information, and exact computation of \(T x=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nT_i x\) using \(n\) component calls. These capabilities are not implied by access only to fresh unbiased samples. Therefore a stochastic bound expressed through \(\sigma\) cannot generally be converted into a finite-sum bound by substituting \(n\), and a finite-sum rate exploiting component reuse does not automatically extend to the online stochastic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fresh stochastic samples and reusable indexed components expose different information. Their oracle complexities cannot generally be converted by replacing variance with dataset size unless an explicit oracle reduction is available.
knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic-to-Finite-Sum Oracle Separation

children.title: Nonexpansive Regimes
children.top_down_role: Halpern applicability for nonexpansive fixed-point maps.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection Characterization of the Halpern Limit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational characterization of the fixed point selected by the anchor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonexpansive map \(T\) on a nonempty closed convex subset of a Hilbert space, the nonempty fixed-point set \(F\) is closed and convex. Hence \(p=P_Fu\) is uniquely characterized by \[p\in F\quad\text{and}\quad\langle u-p,z-p\rangle\leq0\quad\text{for every }z\in F.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The anchor-selected fixed point is certified by fixed-point feasibility and the metric-projection variational inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is closed and convex, and the displayed variational inequality uniquely characterizes \(P_Fu\).
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Characterization of the Halpern Limit

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical sufficient Hilbert-space convergence theorem for the direct nonexpansive regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space, let \(T:C\to C\) be nonexpansive with \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\), and let \(u,x_0\in C\). If \(\alpha_k\in(0,1)\), \(\alpha_k\to0\), \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k=\infty\), and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}|\alpha_{k+1}-\alpha_k|<\infty\), then \[x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)Tx_k\] converges strongly to \(P_Fu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under vanishing, nonsummable, bounded-variation anchor weights, Halpern iteration converges strongly to the fixed point nearest the anchor.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.

notation.meaning: metric projection of the anchor onto the fixed-point set

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Convergence of Halpern Iteration

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and \(T:C\to C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Halpern fixed-point regime requires \(\|Tx-Ty\|\le\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in C\), together with \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the standard Hilbert-space definition of a nonexpansive fixed-point regime.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct Hilbert-space regime for applying Halpern fixed-point iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The operator lies in the nonexpansive Halpern regime precisely when \[\|Tx-Ty\|\le\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C,\] and \(\operatorname{Fix}T:=\{x\in C:Tx=x\}\) is nonempty. For an anchor \(u\in C\), weights \(\alpha_k\in[0,1]\), and \(x_0\in C\), the update \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)Tx_k\) remains in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonexpansive Halpern regime consists of a nonexpansive self-map on a closed convex set with at least one fixed point.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonexpansive Regimes

children.title: Cocoercive Regimes
children.top_down_role: Halpern applicability under cocoercive operator structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint and class-sharp boundary for forward-step nonexpansiveness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(B\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive, then \(I-\gamma B\) is nonexpansive for \(0\leq\gamma\leq2\beta\). This interval is class-sharp: for \(B=\beta^{-1}I\), \[\|(I-\gamma B)x-(I-\gamma B)y\|=|1-\gamma/\beta|\|x-y\|,\] so every \(\gamma>2\beta\) makes the forward map expansive. At \(\gamma=0\), nonexpansiveness holds but the fixed-point/zero-set equivalence generally does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonexpansive step interval ends sharply at 2 beta; the zero step is nonexpansive but does not represent the zero problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I-\gamma B\) is nonexpansive for \(0\leq\gamma\leq2\beta\), and the upper boundary is class-sharp.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Cocoercive Step-Size Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-step structural refinement of the cocoercive Halpern regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(B:H\to H\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive and \(0<\gamma<2\beta\), then \(T=I-\gamma B\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged with \(\alpha=\gamma/(2\beta)\). Equivalently, \[\|Tx-Ty\|^2\leq\|x-y\|^2-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\|(I-T)x-(I-T)y\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict forward step of a beta-cocoercive operator is gamma-over-2-beta averaged, which is stronger than nonexpansiveness.
knowledge_statements.title: Averaged Forward-Step Representation

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, and \(B:H\to H\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive for some \(\beta>0\): \[\langle Bx-By,x-y\rangle\ge \beta\|Bx-By\|^2\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in H.\]
The step size satisfies \(0<\gamma<2\beta\), and \(T:=I-\gamma B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \(T\) is nonexpansive and satisfies \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\operatorname{zer}B\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: cocoercivity makes the forward step nonexpansive for step sizes below twice the cocoercivity constant.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer from cocoercive zero finding to a nonexpansive forward fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\gamma<2\beta\), the forward map \(T=I-\gamma B\) is nonexpansive: \[\|Tx-Ty\|\le \|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in H.\] Its fixed-point set is \[\operatorname{Fix}T=\operatorname{zer}B:=\{x\in H:Bx=0\}.\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{zer}B\ne\varnothing\) places this forward map in the nonexpansive Halpern regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a beta-cocoercive operator and a step size strictly between zero and 2 beta, the forward map is nonexpansive and its fixed points are exactly the operator's zeros.
knowledge_statements.title: Cocoercive Regimes

children.title: Monotone Regimes
children.top_down_role: Halpern applicability for monotone-inclusion realizations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cocoercive single-valued representation induced by a maximal-monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For maximally monotone \(A\) and \(\gamma>0\), the Yosida approximation \(A_\gamma:=\gamma^{-1}(I-J_{\gamma A})\) is single-valued and \(\gamma\)-cocoercive, with \(\operatorname{zer}A_\gamma=\operatorname{zer}A\). Consequently, for \(0<\lambda\leq2\gamma\), \(I-\lambda A_\gamma\) is nonexpansive and has fixed-point set \(\operatorname{zer}A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Yosida approximation converts a maximal-monotone inclusion into a cocoercive zero problem and a nonexpansive forward fixed-point problem.

notation.meaning: forward step applied to the Yosida approximation

knowledge_statements.title: Yosida Forward-Step Route

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternative nonexpansive realization of a maximal-monotone zero problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone and \(\gamma>0\). The reflected resolvent \(R_{\gamma A}:=2J_{\gamma A}-I\) is nonexpansive and \[\operatorname{Fix}R_{\gamma A}=\operatorname{Fix}J_{\gamma A}=\operatorname{zer}A.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonexpansive reflected resolvent represents the same maximal-monotone zero set as the firmly nonexpansive resolvent.
knowledge_statements.title: Reflected-Resolvent Halpern Realization

assumptions_latex: \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space and \(\gamma>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resolvent \(J_{\gamma A}\) is firmly nonexpansive and \(\operatorname{Fix}J_{\gamma A}=\operatorname{zer}A\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the resolvent representation is standard maximal-monotone operator theory.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent transfer from maximal-monotone inclusions to firmly nonexpansive fixed-point problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The resolvent \(J_{\gamma A}:=(I+\gamma A)^{-1}\) is single-valued on \(H\) and satisfies \[\|J_{\gamma A}x-J_{\gamma A}y\|^2\le\langle J_{\gamma A}x-J_{\gamma A}y,x-y\rangle.\] It is therefore firmly nonexpansive, hence nonexpansive. In addition, \[0\in Ax\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=J_{\gamma A}x,\] so \(\operatorname{zer}A=\operatorname{Fix}J_{\gamma A}\). Halpern iteration may consequently be applied to the resolvent when the zero set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent of a maximally monotone operator is firmly nonexpansive, and solving the inclusion is equivalent to finding a resolvent fixed point.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Regimes

children.title: Operator-Regime Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on transferring residual guarantees among the three regimes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact boundary between operator cocoercivity and nonexpansive forward geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B:H\to H\) and \(\gamma>0\). The forward map \(T=I-\gamma B\) is nonexpansive if and only if \(B\) is \(\gamma/2\)-cocoercive: \[\langle Bx-By,x-y\rangle\geq\frac{\gamma}{2}\|Bx-By\|^2\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in H.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed positive step, forward-map nonexpansiveness is exactly equivalent to gamma-over-two cocoercivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I-\gamma B\) is nonexpansive if and only if \(B\) is \(\gamma/2\)-cocoercive.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Forward-Step Transfer Criterion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Cocoercivity of a Nonexpansive Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-way transfer valid for every nonexpansive fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(T:H\to H\) is nonexpansive and \(R:=I-T\), then \(R\) is \(1/2\)-cocoercive: \[\langle Rx-Ry,x-y\rangle\geq\frac12\|Rx-Ry\|^2\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in H.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonexpansive map has a one-half-cocoercive fixed-point residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Cocoercivity of a Nonexpansive Map

assumptions_latex: \(H=\mathbb R^2\) has its Euclidean inner product, and \(B:H\to H\) is defined by \(B(x_1,x_2)=(-x_2,x_1)\).
The step size satisfies \(\gamma>0\), and \(T:=I-\gamma B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The operator \(B\) is monotone, whereas \(T\) is expansive for every \(\gamma>0\); hence monotonicity alone does not imply nonexpansiveness of a forward step.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a skew linear quarter-turn is a direct counterexample to transfer from monotonicity to forward-step nonexpansiveness.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample marking the failure of direct forward-step transfer under mere monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear quarter-turn \(B(x_1,x_2)=(-x_2,x_1)\) is monotone because \[\langle Bx-By,x-y\rangle=0\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in H.\] For every \(\gamma>0\), its forward map \(T=I-\gamma B\) satisfies \[\|Tx-Ty\|^2=(1+\gamma^2)\|x-y\|^2\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in H.\] Thus \(T\) is expansive whenever \(x\ne y\). This counterexample shows that mere monotonicity does not transfer a forward step into the nonexpansive Halpern regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The monotone quarter-turn operator makes every positive forward step expansive, providing a counterexample to forward-step nonexpansiveness under mere monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.title: Operator-Regime Transfer Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Summable Anchor Weights Can Preserve Oscillation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity boundary for divergent total anchor mass in universal Halpern convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\mathbb R\), \(T=-I\), \(u=0\), and \(x_0\ne0\). If \(0<\alpha_k<1\) and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k<\infty\), then \[x_k=(-1)^k\left(\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-\alpha_j)\right)x_0.\] The infinite product is positive, so \((x_k)\) oscillates with nonvanishing magnitude and does not converge to the unique fixed point \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the reflection T=-I, summable anchor weights leave a nonvanishing alternating component, preventing convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Halpern sequence does not converge to \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Summable Anchor Weights Can Preserve Oscillation

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(T:H\to H\) is nonexpansive, and \(\operatorname{Fix}T\ne\varnothing\).
The exact Halpern iteration is \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)Tx_k\), where \(u,x_0\in H\) and \(0\leq\alpha_k\leq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A schedule with \(\limsup_{k\to\infty}\alpha_k>0\) is not universally admissible for convergence to a fixed point. In particular, take \(H=\mathbb R\), \(T(x)=0\), \(u\ne0\), and \(\alpha_k\equiv a\in(0,1)\). Then \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}\), but \(x_{k+1}=au\) for every \(k\), so the iterates converge to \(au\notin\operatorname{Fix}T\). Thus the standard requirement \(\alpha_k\to0\) cannot be removed from a universal Halpern convergence theorem.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the one-dimensional constant-operator counterexample follows by direct substitution into the Halpern recurrence
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary vanishing-weight boundary for exact Hilbert-space Halpern iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the Halpern recurrence \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)Tx_k\), convergence for every nonexpansive \(T\) with a fixed point requires restrictions on the anchor schedule beyond \(0\leq\alpha_k\leq1\). A schedule bounded away from zero can retain a permanent anchor bias. Indeed, with \(T(x)=0\) on \(\mathbb R\), \(u\ne0\), and \(\alpha_k\equiv a\in(0,1)\), one has \(x_{k+1}=au\), whereas the unique fixed point is \(0\). Hence such a schedule is inadmissible for universal fixed-point convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anchor weights that do not vanish can leave a permanent bias: for the zero operator and a constant positive weight, Halpern iterates converge away from the unique fixed point.
knowledge_statements.title: Inadmissible Anchor Schedules

children.title: Loss of Nonexpansiveness
children.top_down_role: Residual behavior after the fixed-point map leaves the nonexpansive regime.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}\), the recurrence satisfies \(x_k=2^k x_0/(k+1)\), and therefore \(|x_k|\to\infty\). Thus standard Halpern weights do not compensate for the loss of nonexpansiveness.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the displayed divergence formula is obtained by multiplying the scalar recurrence factors
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit expansive-operator obstruction under otherwise standard Halpern weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Nonexpansiveness is essential for a universal Halpern convergence guarantee. Let \(T(x)=2x\) on \(\mathbb R\), so \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}\), and choose \(u=0\), \(x_0\ne0\), and \(\alpha_k=1/(k+2)\). Then \(x_{k+1}=2(k+1)x_k/(k+2)\), whence \(x_k=2^k x_0/(k+1)\). Consequently \(|x_k|\to\infty\), despite \(\alpha_k\to0\) and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k=\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the expansive map T(x)=2x, standard Halpern weights produce exponentially diverging iterates, even though the operator has the fixed point zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Nonexpansiveness

children.title: Persistent Inexactness
children.top_down_role: Residual behavior under nonvanishing evaluation error.

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a nonzero real Hilbert space, \(T(x)=0\), and the inexact evaluation is \(Tx_k+e_k\).
The iteration is \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)(Tx_k+e_k)\), with \(\alpha_k\to0\) and \(e_k\equiv e\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterates satisfy \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)e\to e\), while \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}\). Persistent nonvanishing evaluation error can therefore destroy fixed-point convergence even for a firmly nonexpansive operator.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the constant-error counterexample is an immediate evaluation of the inexact recurrence
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonvanishing additive evaluation errors in an inexact Halpern recurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Vanishing anchor weights do not suppress a persistent additive operator error. Let \(T(x)=0\) on a nonzero Hilbert space \(H\), and use the inexact recurrence \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)(Tx_k+e_k)\). If \(\alpha_k\to0\) and \(e_k=e\ne0\) for all \(k\), then \(x_{k+1}=\alpha_k u+(1-\alpha_k)e\to e\). Since \(\operatorname{Fix}T=\{0\}\), the limit is not a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant operator-evaluation error survives vanishing Halpern anchor weights and can force convergence to a nonfixed point, even for the zero operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Inexactness

children.title: Compounded Geometry-Error Failure
children.top_down_role: Failure boundaries where geometric instability interacts with persistent error.

assumptions_latex: The inexact recurrence uses the persistent error \(e_k\equiv e\), with initial value \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recurrence is \(x_{k+1}=2(k+1)x_k/(k+2)+(k+1)e/(k+2)\). Its rescaling \(y_k=(k+1)x_k/2^k\) satisfies \(y_{k+1}=y_k+e(k+1)/2^{k+1}\), so \(y_k\to x_0+2e\). Unless \(x_0=-2e\), \(|x_k|\) grows on the order of \(2^k/k\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the coupled failure and exceptional initial value follow from the explicitly solved scalar recurrence
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar example coupling expansive geometry with persistent evaluation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Geometry and error failures may compound rather than merely add. For \(T(x)=2x\), \(u=0\), \(\alpha_k=1/(k+2)\), and \(e_k=e\), the inexact Halpern recurrence becomes \(x_{k+1}=2(k+1)x_k/(k+2)+(k+1)e/(k+2)\). Defining \(y_k=(k+1)x_k/2^k\) gives \(y_{k+1}=y_k+e(k+1)/2^{k+1}\), hence \(y_k\to x_0+2e\). Except for the tuned value \(x_0=-2e\), the iterates diverge at order \(2^k/k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With both an expansive operator and persistent error, inexact Halpern iterates generally diverge exponentially; only one specially tuned initial value avoids the dominant term.
knowledge_statements.title: Compounded Geometry-Error Failure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard sufficient condition for converting residual rates into distance-to-solution rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\) and \(R=I-T\). Suppose that locally \[\operatorname{dist}(x,F)\leq\kappa\|Rx\|.\] Then every sequence in that neighborhood satisfying \(\|Rx_k\|\leq\varepsilon_k\) also satisfies \[\operatorname{dist}(x_k,F)\leq\kappa\varepsilon_k.\] Thus a pointwise residual rate transfers with the same order to distance from the fixed-point set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local metric-subregularity error bound is sufficient to transfer a residual rate to the same-order distance-to-fixed-set rate.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Subregularity Rate Transfer

assumptions_latex: The fixed-point residual is \(r(x)=x-T(x)\), and distance is measured to \(F=\operatorname{Fix}T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \(T\) is nonexpansive, \(F=\{0\}\), and \(r(x)=x^2/(1+x)\). Hence \(r(x)/\operatorname{dist}(x,F)=x/(1+x)\to0\) as \(x\downarrow0\). Consequently, a fast residual rate alone cannot yield the same rate for iterate distance without an error bound such as metric subregularity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of residual rates to transfer to iterate-distance rates without an error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Residual decay need not imply comparable acceleration of the iterates. Define \(T(x)=x/(1+x)\) on \([0,\infty)\). Since \(0\leq T'(x)\leq1\), the map is nonexpansive, and its fixed-point set is \(F=\{0\}\). Its residual is \(r(x)=x-T(x)=x^2/(1+x)\), whereas \(\operatorname{dist}(x,F)=x\). Therefore \(r(x)/\operatorname{dist}(x,F)=x/(1+x)\to0\) as \(x\downarrow0\); no local constant can convert residual decay into an equal iterate-distance rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonexpansive map can have a residual quadratically smaller than fixed-point distance, so accelerated residual decay need not accelerate the iterates without an error bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Acceleration without Iterate Acceleration

children.title: Ergodic Residual Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity guarantees for averaged residual certificates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition needed for telescoping to yield ergodic decay.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Since \(\bar r_N=(x_0-x_{N+1})/\Lambda_N\), decay requires \(\|x_0-x_{N+1}\|/\Lambda_N\to0\). With \(\lambda_k=1\), \(r_k=u\), and \(x_{k+1}=x_k-u\), one has \(\Lambda_N=N+1\), \(\|x_0-x_{N+1}\|=N+1\), and \(\bar r_N=u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cumulative-weight growth alone gives no decay if endpoint displacement grows at the same scale.
knowledge_statements.title: Endpoint and Weight Growth Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharpness of the Endpoint Ergodic Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact attainment of the endpoint-displacement estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(D\geq0\), positive weights \(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_N\), and a unit vector \(u\). Let \(r_k=(D/\Lambda_N)u\) and \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\lambda_k r_k\). Then \(x_0-x_{N+1}=Du\) and \(\bar r_N=(D/\Lambda_N)u\). Hence \(\|\bar r_N\|=D/\Lambda_N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant aligned residual sequence attains the endpoint ergodic bound exactly.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Endpoint Ergodic Bound

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a Hilbert space and \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\lambda_k r_k\), where \(r_k\in H\) and \(\lambda_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The weighted ergodic residual \(\bar r_N=\Lambda_N^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^N\lambda_k r_k\) obeys \(\|\bar r_N\|\leq D/\Lambda_N\). If \(\lambda_k\geq\underline\lambda>0\), then \(\|\bar r_N\|\leq D/((N+1)\underline\lambda)\), so attaining \(\|\bar r_N\|\leq\varepsilon\) requires at most order \(1/\varepsilon\) iterations under this endpoint bound.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the bound follows from telescoping the stated residual-form iteration and applying the norm inequality
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint-bounded residual-form iteration with positive weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Summing \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\lambda_k r_k\) yields \(\sum_{k=0}^N\lambda_k r_k=x_0-x_{N+1}\). Thus, for \(\Lambda_N=\sum_{k=0}^N\lambda_k\), the ergodic residual \(\bar r_N=\Lambda_N^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^N\lambda_k r_k\) satisfies \(\|\bar r_N\|\leq D/\Lambda_N\) whenever \(\|x_0-x_{N+1}\|\leq D\). If every \(\lambda_k\geq\underline\lambda>0\), then \(\|\bar r_N\|\leq D/((N+1)\underline\lambda)\), giving \(O(1/N)\) ergodic residual decay.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Telescoping a residual-form iteration gives an ergodic residual bounded by endpoint displacement over cumulative step size, hence an O(1/N) rate for uniformly positive steps.
knowledge_statements.title: Ergodic Residual Complexity

children.title: Best-Iterate Residual Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity guarantees based on the best residual observed within a horizon.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cumulative Weight Growth Is Necessary for Residual Decay
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the weighted-energy complexity conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The estimate \(\min_{k\leq N}\|r_k\|\leq\sqrt{E/\Lambda_N}\) implies decay only if \(\Lambda_N\to\infty\). If \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty\lambda_k=\Lambda_\infty<\infty\), the sequence \(r_k=\sqrt{E/\Lambda_\infty}\,u\) satisfies every finite weighted energy bound but its best residual remains positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded total weight permits bounded residual energy while every residual stays uniformly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A weighted energy bound does not imply \(\min_{k\leq N}\|r_k\|\to0\) when \(\Lambda_N\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Cumulative Weight Growth Is Necessary for Residual Decay

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharpness of the Weighted Best-Iterate Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case exactness of the minimum-versus-energy estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For positive weights \(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_N\), \(\Lambda_N=\sum_{k=0}^N\lambda_k\), and \(E\geq0\), choose a unit vector \(u\) and set \(r_k=\sqrt{E/\Lambda_N}\,u\). Then \[\sum_{k=0}^N\lambda_k\|r_k\|^2=E,\qquad\min_{0\leq k\leq N}\|r_k\|=\sqrt{E/\Lambda_N}.\] Hence no better worst-case bound follows from the weighted energy estimate alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal residual magnitudes attain the weighted best-iterate estimate exactly.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Weighted Best-Iterate Bound
Best-Iterate Residual Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best residual selected from a finite prefix using a weighted energy estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\sum_{k=0}^N\lambda_k\|r_k\|^2\leq E\) and \(\Lambda_N=\sum_{k=0}^N\lambda_k\), then \(\Lambda_N\min_{0\leq k\leq N}\|r_k\|^2\leq E\). Consequently, some \(j_N\in\{0,\ldots,N\}\) satisfies \(\|r_{j_N}\|\leq\sqrt{E/\Lambda_N}\). When \(\lambda_k\geq\underline\lambda>0\), this becomes \(\min_{0\leq k\leq N}\|r_k\|\leq\sqrt{E/((N+1)\underline\lambda)}\), an \(O(N^{-1/2})\) best-iterate bound and an \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) iteration complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted residual-energy bound guarantees one iterate with residual O(1/sqrt(N)); finding an epsilon residual therefore takes O(1/epsilon squared) iterations.
assumptions_latex: Residuals \(r_0,\ldots,r_N\) lie in a Hilbert space, and weights \(\lambda_k>0\) satisfy \(\Lambda_N=\sum_{k=0}^N\lambda_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(j_N\in\{0,\ldots,N\}\) such that \(\|r_{j_N}\|\leq\sqrt{E/\Lambda_N}\). If \(\lambda_k\geq\underline\lambda>0\), then \(\min_{0\leq k\leq N}\|r_k\|\leq\sqrt{E/((N+1)\underline\lambda)}\), requiring order \(1/\varepsilon^2\) iterations to produce a residual at most \(\varepsilon\).
